units.excerpt: In September 2023, we released our Responsible Scaling Policy (RSP), a public commitment not to train or deploy models capable of causing catastrophic harm unless we have implemented safety and security measures that will keep risks below acceptable levels.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic describes its September 2023 RSP as a public commitment not to train or deploy catastrophically dangerous models absent adequate safety and security measures.

units.excerpt: We are now updating our RSP to account for the lessons we've learned over the last year. This updated policy reflects our view that risk governance in this rapidly evolving domain should be proportional, iterative, and exportable.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic is updating the RSP based on lessons learned, guided by principles of proportionality, iteration, and exportability.

units.excerpt: Background. AI Safety Level Standards (ASL Standards) are a set of technical and operational measures for safely training and deploying frontier AI models. These currently fall into two categories: Deployment Standards and Security Standards.
units.paraphrase: ASL Standards are technical and operational measures for safe training and deployment, currently divided into Deployment and Security Standards.

units.excerpt: As model capabilities increase, so will the need for stronger safeguards, which are captured in successively higher ASL Standards. At present, all of our models must meet the ASL-2 Deployment and Security Standards.
units.paraphrase: Stronger safeguards are needed as capabilities increase, and currently all models must meet ASL-2 standards.

units.excerpt: To determine when a model has become sufficiently advanced such that its deployment and security measures should be strengthened, we use the concepts of Capability Thresholds and Required Safeguards. A Capability Threshold tells us when we need to upgrade our protections, and the corresponding Required Safeguards tell us what standard should apply.
units.paraphrase: Capability Thresholds signal when protections need upgrading, and Required Safeguards specify what standard applies.

units.excerpt: Capability Thresholds and Required Safeguards. The Required Safeguards for each Capability Threshold are intended to mitigate risk to acceptable levels.
units.paraphrase: Required Safeguards for each Capability Threshold aim to mitigate risk to acceptable levels.

units.excerpt: This update to our RSP provides specifications for Capabilities Thresholds related to Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear (CBRN) weapons and Autonomous AI Research and Development (AI R&D) and identifies the corresponding Required Safeguards.
units.paraphrase: This RSP update specifies Capability Thresholds for CBRN weapons and Autonomous AI R&D, along with their Required Safeguards.

units.excerpt: Capability assessment. We will routinely test models to determine whether their capabilities fall sufficiently far below the Capability Thresholds such that the ASL-2 Standard remains appropriate.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic commits to routine testing to check whether models remain sufficiently below Capability Thresholds under ASL-2.

units.excerpt: We will first conduct preliminary assessments to determine whether a more comprehensive evaluation is needed. For models requiring comprehensive testing, we will assess whether the model is unlikely to reach any relevant Capability Thresholds absent surprising advances in widely accessible post-training enhancements.
units.paraphrase: Preliminary assessments determine whether comprehensive testing is needed; comprehensive testing assesses distance from Capability Thresholds barring surprising post-training advances.

units.excerpt: If, after the comprehensive testing, we determine that the model is sufficiently below the relevant Capability Thresholds, then we will continue to apply the ASL-2 Standard.
units.paraphrase: If comprehensive testing shows the model remains sufficiently below thresholds, ASL-2 continues to apply.

units.excerpt: If, however, we are unable to make the required showing, we will act as though the model has surpassed the Capability Threshold. This means that we will both upgrade to the ASL-3 Required Safeguards and conduct a follow-up capability assessment to confirm that the ASL-4 Standard is not necessary.
units.paraphrase: If the required showing cannot be made, the model is treated as having surpassed the threshold, triggering an ASL-3 upgrade and a follow-up assessment for ASL-4 necessity.

units.excerpt: Safeguards assessment. To determine whether the measures we have adopted satisfy the ASL-3 Required Safeguards, we will conduct a safeguards assessment.
units.paraphrase: A safeguards assessment determines whether adopted measures satisfy ASL-3 Required Safeguards.

units.excerpt: For the ASL-3 Deployment Standard, we will evaluate whether it is robust to persistent attempts to misuse the capability in question. For the ASL-3 Security Standard, we will evaluate whether it is highly protected against non-state attackers attempting to steal model weights.
units.paraphrase: ASL-3 Deployment is evaluated for robustness to persistent misuse attempts, and ASL-3 Security for protection against non-state weight theft.

units.excerpt: If we determine that we have met the ASL-3 Required Safeguards, then we will proceed to deployment, provided we have also conducted a follow-up capability assessment.
units.paraphrase: Meeting ASL-3 Required Safeguards permits deployment, conditional on a follow-up capability assessment also having been conducted.

units.excerpt: Follow-up capability assessment. In parallel with upgrading a model to the ASL-3 Required Safeguards, we will conduct a follow-up capability assessment to confirm that further safeguards are not necessary.
units.paraphrase: A follow-up capability assessment runs alongside the ASL-3 upgrade to confirm no further safeguards are needed.

units.excerpt: Deployment and scaling outcomes. We may deploy or store a model if either of the following criteria are met: (1) the model's capabilities are sufficiently far away from the existing Capability Thresholds, making the current ASL-2 Standard appropriate;
units.paraphrase: Deployment or storage is permitted if the model's capabilities remain sufficiently far from thresholds under ASL-2.

units.context_stem: Deployment and scaling outcomes. We may deploy or store a model if either of the following criteria are met:
units.excerpt: or (2) the model's capabilities have surpassed the existing Capabilities Threshold, but we have implemented the ASL-3 Required Safeguards and conducted the follow-up capability assessment.
units.paraphrase: Alternatively, deployment or storage is permitted once ASL-3 Required Safeguards are implemented and the follow-up capability assessment is complete, even if the threshold is surpassed.

units.excerpt: In any scenario where we determine that a model requires ASL-3 Required Safeguards but we are unable to implement them immediately, we will act promptly to reduce interim risk to acceptable levels until the ASL-3 Required Safeguards are in place.
units.paraphrase: If ASL-3 Required Safeguards are needed but cannot be implemented immediately, Anthropic will act promptly to reduce interim risk until they are in place.

units.excerpt: Governance and transparency. To facilitate the effective implementation of this policy across the company, we commit to several internal governance measures, including maintaining the position of Responsible Scaling Officer, establishing a process through which Anthropic staff may anonymously notify the Responsible Scaling Officer of any potential instances of noncompliance, and developing internal safety procedures for incident scenarios.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic commits to internal governance measures including a Responsible Scaling Officer role, an anonymous noncompliance reporting process, and internal incident procedures.

units.excerpt: To advance the public dialogue on the regulation of frontier AI model risks and to enable examination of our actions, we will also publicly release key materials related to the evaluation and deployment of our models with sensitive information removed and solicit input from external experts in relevant domains.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will publicly release evaluation and deployment materials (with sensitive information redacted) and seek external expert input to support public dialogue and scrutiny.

units.excerpt: As frontier AI models advance, we believe they will bring about transformative benefits for our society and economy. AI could accelerate scientific discoveries, revolutionize healthcare, enhance our education system, and create entirely new domains for human creativity and innovation.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic believes advancing frontier AI models will bring transformative societal and economic benefits across science, healthcare, education, and creativity.

units.excerpt: Frontier AI models also, however, present new challenges and risks that warrant careful study and effective safeguards.
units.paraphrase: Frontier AI models also present new risks requiring careful study and effective safeguards.

units.excerpt: In September 2023, we released our Responsible Scaling Policy (RSP), a first-of-its-kind public commitment not to train or deploy models capable of causing catastrophic harm unless we have implemented safety and security measures that will keep risks below acceptable levels.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic released the RSP in September 2023 as a first-of-its-kind commitment against training or deploying catastrophically harmful models without adequate safeguards.

units.excerpt: Our RSP serves several purposes: it is an internal operating procedure for investigating and mitigating these risks and helps inform the public of our plans and commitments.
units.paraphrase: The RSP functions both as an internal operating procedure and as public communication of Anthropic's plans and commitments.

units.excerpt: We also hope it will serve as a prototype for other companies looking to adopt similar frameworks and, potentially, inform regulators about possible best practices.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic hopes the RSP will serve as a model for other companies and inform regulatory best practices.

units.excerpt: We are now updating our RSP to account for the lessons we've learned over the last year. This policy reflects our view that risk governance in this rapidly evolving domain should be proportional, iterative, and exportable.
units.paraphrase: The RSP is being updated based on lessons learned, reflecting principles of proportionality, iteration, and exportability.

units.excerpt: First, our approach to risk should be proportional. Central to our policy is the concept of AI Safety Level Standards: technical and operational standards for safely training and deploying frontier models that correspond with a particular level of risk.
units.paraphrase: Risk approach should be proportional, centered on AI Safety Level Standards tied to risk levels.

units.excerpt: By implementing safeguards that are proportional to the nature and extent of an AI model's risks, we can balance innovation with safety, maintaining rigorous protections without unnecessarily hindering progress.
units.paraphrase: Proportional safeguards balance innovation and safety without unduly hindering progress.

units.excerpt: This approach also enables us to allocate resources efficiently, focusing our most stringent safeguards on the models that pose the greater risk, while affording more flexibility for lower-risk systems.
units.paraphrase: Proportionality allows efficient resource allocation, concentrating stringent safeguards on higher-risk models while allowing flexibility for lower-risk ones.

units.excerpt: Second, our approach to risk should be iterative. Since the frontier of AI is rapidly evolving, we cannot anticipate what safety and security measures will be appropriate for models far beyond the current frontier.
units.paraphrase: The risk approach should be iterative because rapid AI advancement makes it hard to anticipate future safety needs.

units.excerpt: We will thus regularly measure the capability of our models and adjust our safeguards accordingly. Further, we will continue to research potential risks and next-generation mitigation techniques.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will regularly measure model capability, adjust safeguards, and continue researching risks and mitigation techniques.

units.excerpt: And, at the highest level of generality, we will look for opportunities to improve and strengthen our overarching risk management framework.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will seek opportunities to improve its overall risk management framework.

units.excerpt: Third, our approach to risk should be exportable. To demonstrate that it is possible to balance innovation with safety, we must put forward our proof of concept: a pragmatic, flexible, and scalable approach to risk governance.
units.paraphrase: The risk approach should be exportable, offering a pragmatic proof-of-concept that innovation and safety can coexist.

units.excerpt: By sharing our approach externally, we aim to set a new industry standard that encourages widespread adoption of similar frameworks.
units.paraphrase: Sharing the approach externally aims to set an industry standard encouraging wider adoption.

units.excerpt: In the long term, we hope that our policy may offer relevant insights for regulation. In the meantime, we will continue to share our findings with policymakers.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic hopes the policy will inform regulation long-term and commits to sharing findings with policymakers in the interim.

units.excerpt: Although this policy focuses on catastrophic risks, they are not the only risks that we consider important.
units.paraphrase: Catastrophic risks are the focus, but not the only risks Anthropic considers important.

units.excerpt: Our Usage Policy sets forth our standards for the use of our products, including prohibitions on using our models to spread misinformation, incite violence or hateful behavior, or engage in fraudulent or abusive practices, and we continually refine our technical measures for enforcing our trust and safety standards at scale.
units.paraphrase: The Usage Policy prohibits misuse such as misinformation, incitement, and fraud, and enforcement measures are continually refined.

units.excerpt: Further, we conduct research to understand the broader societal impacts of our models. Our Responsible Scaling Policy complements our work in these areas, contributing to our understanding of current and potential risks.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic conducts research on societal impacts, which the RSP complements by contributing to risk understanding.

units.excerpt: At Anthropic, we are committed to developing AI responsibly and transparently. Since our founding, we have recognized the importance of proactively addressing potential risks as we push the boundaries of AI capability and of clearly communicating about the nature and extent of those risks.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic is committed to responsible, transparent AI development, proactively addressing risks and communicating clearly since its founding.

units.excerpt: We look forward to continuing to refine our approach to risk governance and to collaborating with stakeholders across the AI ecosystem.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic looks forward to refining its risk governance approach and collaborating with ecosystem stakeholders.

units.excerpt: This policy is designed in the spirit of the Responsible Scaling Policy (RSP) framework introduced by the non-profit AI safety organization METR, as well as emerging government policy proposals in the UK, EU, and US.
units.paraphrase: The policy draws on METR's RSP framework and emerging UK, EU, and US government policy proposals.

units.excerpt: This policy also helps satisfy our Voluntary White House Commitments (2023) and Frontier AI Safety Commitments (2024).
units.paraphrase: The policy also helps meet Anthropic's Voluntary White House Commitments and Frontier AI Safety Commitments.

units.excerpt: We extend our sincere gratitude to the many external groups that provided invaluable guidance on the development and refinement of our Responsible Scaling Policy.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic thanks external groups for guidance on developing and refining the RSP.

units.excerpt: We actively welcome feedback on our policy and suggestions for improvement from other entities engaged in frontier AI risk evaluations or safety and security standards. To submit your feedback or suggestions, please contact us at rsp@anthropic.com.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic welcomes feedback from other entities working on frontier AI risk and safety standards, via a provided contact email.

units.excerpt: AI Safety Level Standards (ASL Standards) are core to our risk mitigation strategy. An ASL Standard is a set of technical and operational measures for safely training and deploying frontier AI models.
units.paraphrase: ASL Standards, central to the risk mitigation strategy, are technical and operational measures for safe training and deployment.

units.excerpt: As model capabilities increase, so will the need for stronger safeguards, which are captured in successively higher ASL Standards. Definitions of ASL Standards and other key terms are available in Appendix A.
units.paraphrase: Increasing capabilities require stronger safeguards via higher ASL Standards; definitions appear in Appendix A.

units.excerpt: The types of measures that compose an ASL Standard currently fall into two categories–Deployment Standards and Security Standards–which map onto the types of risks that frontier AI models may pose.
units.paraphrase: ASL Standard measures fall into two categories, Deployment and Security Standards, corresponding to different risk types.

units.excerpt: Deployment Standards: Deployment Standards are technical, operational, and policy measures to ensure the safe usage of AI models by external users (i.e., our users and customers) as well as internal users (i.e., our employees).
units.paraphrase: Deployment Standards are measures ensuring safe use of AI models by both external and internal users.

units.excerpt: Deployment Standards aim to strike a balance between enabling beneficial use of AI technologies and mitigating the risks of potentially catastrophic cases of misuse.
units.paraphrase: Deployment Standards balance beneficial AI use against risks of catastrophic misuse.

units.excerpt: Security Standards: Security Standards are technical, operational, and policy measures to protect AI models–particularly their weights and associated systems–from unauthorized access, theft, or compromise by malicious actors.
units.paraphrase: Security Standards protect AI models, especially their weights, from unauthorized access, theft, or compromise.

units.excerpt: Security Standards are intended to maintain the integrity and controlled use of AI models throughout their lifecycle, from development to deployment.
units.paraphrase: Security Standards aim to maintain integrity and controlled use of models across their lifecycle.

units.excerpt: We expect to continue refining our framework in response to future risks (for example, the risk that an AI system attempts to subvert the goals of its operators).
units.paraphrase: Anthropic expects to continue refining the framework in response to future risks, such as AI subverting operator goals.

units.excerpt: At present, all of our models must meet the ASL-2 Deployment and Security Standards. The ASL-2 Security and Deployment Standards provide a baseline level of safe deployment and model security for AI models.
units.paraphrase: All current models must meet ASL-2 Deployment and Security Standards, which provide a baseline level of safety and security.

units.excerpt: These standards, which are summarized below, are available in full in Appendix B.
units.paraphrase: The ASL-2 standards are summarized here, with full detail in Appendix B.

units.excerpt: The ASL-2 Deployment Standard reduces the prevalence of misuse, and includes the publication of model cards and enforcement of Usage Policy; harmlessness training such as Constitutional AI and automated detection mechanisms; and establishing vulnerability reporting channels as well as a bug bounty for universal jailbreaks.
units.paraphrase: The ASL-2 Deployment Standard reduces misuse via model card publication, Usage Policy enforcement, harmlessness training, detection mechanisms, vulnerability reporting, and a jailbreak bug bounty.

units.excerpt: The ASL-2 Security Standard requires a security system that can likely thwart most opportunistic attackers and includes vendor and supplier security reviews, physical security measures, and the use of secure-by-design principles.
units.paraphrase: The ASL-2 Security Standard requires defenses likely sufficient against most opportunistic attackers, including vendor reviews, physical security, and secure-by-design principles.

units.excerpt: Although the ASL-2 Standard is appropriate for all of our current models, that may not hold true in the future as our models become more capable.
units.paraphrase: ASL-2 currently suffices but may not remain appropriate as models grow more capable.

units.excerpt: To determine when a model has become sufficiently advanced such that its deployment and security measures should be strengthened, we use the concepts of Capability Thresholds and Required Safeguards.
units.paraphrase: Capability Thresholds and Required Safeguards determine when to strengthen deployment and security measures.

units.excerpt: A Capability Threshold tells us when we need to upgrade our protections, and the corresponding Required Safeguards tell us what standard should apply.
units.paraphrase: Capability Thresholds signal upgrade timing, and Required Safeguards specify the applicable standard.

units.excerpt: A Capability Threshold is a prespecified level of AI capability that, if reached, signals (1) a meaningful increase in the level of risk if the model remains under the existing set of safeguards and (2) a corresponding need to upgrade the safeguards to a higher ASL Standard.
units.paraphrase: A Capability Threshold is a prespecified capability level whose attainment signals both increased risk under existing safeguards and the need for upgraded safeguards.

units.excerpt: In other words, a Capability Threshold serves as a trigger for shifting from an ASL-N Standard to an ASL-N+1 Standard (or, in some cases, moving straight to ASL N+2 or higher).
units.paraphrase: A Capability Threshold triggers shifting to the next (or higher) ASL Standard.

units.excerpt: Depending on the Capability Threshold, it may not be necessary to upgrade both the Deployment and Security Standards; each Capability Threshold corresponds to specific Required Safeguards that identify which of the ASL Standards must be met.
units.paraphrase: Not every threshold requires upgrading both Deployment and Security Standards; each threshold's Required Safeguards specify which standards apply.

units.excerpt: Below, we specify the Capability Thresholds and their corresponding Required Safeguards. The Required Safeguards for each Capability Threshold are intended to mitigate risk from a model with such capabilities to acceptable levels.
units.paraphrase: This section specifies Capability Thresholds and their Required Safeguards, aimed at mitigating risk to acceptable levels.

units.excerpt: In developing these standards, we have weighed the risks and benefits of frontier model development. We believe these safeguards are achievable with sufficient investment and advance planning into research and development and would advocate for the industry as a whole to adopt them.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic weighed risks and benefits when developing these standards and believes the safeguards are achievable with sufficient investment, advocating industry-wide adoption.

units.excerpt: We will conduct assessments to inform when to implement the Required Safeguards (see Section 4). The Capability Thresholds summarized below are available in full in Appendix C.
units.paraphrase: Assessments will inform implementation timing of Required Safeguards; full threshold detail is in Appendix C.

units.context_stem: Row: Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear (CBRN) weapons; Column: Capability Thresholds
units.excerpt: CBRN-3: The ability to significantly help individuals or groups with basic technical backgrounds (e.g., undergraduate STEM degrees) create/obtain and deploy CBRN weapons.
units.paraphrase: CBRN-3 threshold is reached when the model can significantly help individuals with basic technical backgrounds create/obtain and deploy CBRN weapons.

units.context_stem: Row: Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear (CBRN) weapons; Column: Required Safeguards; Threshold: CBRN-3
units.excerpt: This capability could greatly increase the number of actors who could cause this sort of damage, and there is no clear reason to expect an offsetting improvement in defensive capabilities.
units.paraphrase: This capability could greatly widen the pool of actors able to cause harm, without a corresponding defensive improvement expected.

units.context_stem: Row: Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear (CBRN) weapons; Column: Required Safeguards; Threshold: CBRN-3
units.excerpt: The ASL-3 Deployment Standard and the ASL-3 Security Standard, which protect against misuse and model-weight theft by non-state adversaries, are required.
units.paraphrase: CBRN-3 requires both the ASL-3 Deployment Standard and ASL-3 Security Standard, protecting against misuse and non-state weight theft.

units.context_stem: Row: Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear (CBRN) weapons; Column: Capability Thresholds
units.excerpt: CBRN-4: The ability to substantially uplift CBRN development capabilities of moderately resourced state programs (with relevant expert teams), such as by novel weapons design, substantially accelerating existing processes, or dramatic reduction in technical barriers.
units.paraphrase: CBRN-4 is reached when the model can substantially uplift moderately resourced state CBRN programs through novel weapon design, acceleration, or lowered technical barriers.

units.context_stem: Row: Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear (CBRN) weapons; Column: Required Safeguards; Threshold: CBRN-4
units.excerpt: We expect this threshold will require the ASL-4 Deployment and Security Standards. We plan to add more information about what those entail in a future update.
units.paraphrase: CBRN-4 is expected to require ASL-4 Deployment and Security Standards, with further detail planned for a future update.

units.locator: Table (untitled) / AI R&D / Capability Threshold / AI R&D-4
units.context_stem: Row: Autonomous AI Research and Development (AI R&D); Column: Capability Thresholds
units.excerpt: AI R&D-4: The ability to fully automate the work of an entry-level, remote-only Researcher at Anthropic.
units.paraphrase: AI R&D-4 is reached when the model can fully automate an entry-level remote researcher's work at Anthropic.

units.locator: Table (untitled) / AI R&D / Required Safeguards / AI R&D-4
units.context_stem: Row: Autonomous AI Research and Development (AI R&D); Column: Required Safeguards; Threshold: AI R&D-4
units.excerpt: The ASL-3 Security Standard is required. In addition, we will develop an affirmative case that (1) identifies the most immediate and relevant risks from models pursuing misaligned goals and (2) explains how we have mitigated these risks to acceptable levels.
units.paraphrase: AI R&D-4 requires the ASL-3 Security Standard plus an affirmative case identifying risks from misaligned goal pursuit and explaining their mitigation.

units.locator: Table (untitled) / AI R&D / Required Safeguards / AI R&D-4
units.context_stem: Row: Autonomous AI Research and Development (AI R&D); Column: Required Safeguards; Threshold: AI R&D-4
units.excerpt: The affirmative case will describe, as relevant, evidence on model capabilities; evidence on AI alignment; mitigations (such as monitoring and other safeguards); and our overall reasoning.
units.paraphrase: The affirmative case covers capability evidence, alignment evidence, mitigations, and overall reasoning.

units.locator: Table (untitled) / AI R&D / Capability Threshold / AI R&D-5
units.context_stem: Row: Autonomous AI Research and Development (AI R&D); Column: Capability Thresholds
units.excerpt: AI R&D-5: The ability to cause dramatic acceleration in the rate of effective scaling
units.paraphrase: AI R&D-5 is reached when the model can dramatically accelerate the rate of effective scaling.

units.locator: Table (untitled) / AI R&D / Required Safeguards / AI R&D-5
units.context_stem: Row: Autonomous AI Research and Development (AI R&D); Column: Required Safeguards; Threshold: AI R&D-5
units.excerpt: At minimum, the ASL-4 Security Standard (which would protect against model-weight theft by state-level adversaries) is required, although we expect a higher security standard may be required.
units.paraphrase: AI R&D-5 requires at least the ASL-4 Security Standard against state-level theft, with a higher standard possibly needed.

units.locator: Table (untitled) / AI R&D / Required Safeguards / AI R&D-5
units.context_stem: Row: Autonomous AI Research and Development (AI R&D); Column: Required Safeguards; Threshold: AI R&D-5
units.excerpt: As with AI R&D-4, we also expect an affirmative case will be required.
units.paraphrase: An affirmative case is also expected to be required for AI R&D-5, as with AI R&D-4.

units.excerpt: These Capability Thresholds represent our current understanding of the most pressing catastrophic risks. As our understanding evolves, we may identify additional thresholds.
units.paraphrase: The listed thresholds reflect current understanding of pressing catastrophic risks, and additional thresholds may be identified as understanding evolves.

units.excerpt: For each threshold, we will identify and describe the corresponding Required Safeguards as soon as feasible, and at minimum before training or deploying any model that reaches that threshold.
units.paraphrase: Required Safeguards for each threshold will be identified as soon as feasible, and no later than before training or deploying a model reaching that threshold.

units.excerpt: We will consider it sufficient to rule out the possibility that a model has surpassed the two Autonomous AI R&D Capability Thresholds by considering an earlier (i.e., less capable) checkpoint: the ability to autonomously perform a wide range of 2-8 hour software engineering tasks.
units.paraphrase: An earlier checkpoint—autonomous performance of 2-8 hour software engineering tasks—suffices to rule out surpassing the two AI R&D thresholds.

units.excerpt: We would view this level of capability as an important checkpoint towards both Autonomous AI R&D as well as other capabilities that may warrant similar attention (for example, autonomous replication).
units.paraphrase: This capability level is seen as an important checkpoint toward AI R&D and other capabilities like autonomous replication.

units.context_stem: We will test for this checkpoint and, by the time we reach it, we will:
units.excerpt: (1) aim to have met (or be close to meeting) the ASL-3 Security Standard as an intermediate goal;
units.paraphrase: By the time the checkpoint is reached, Anthropic aims to have met or nearly met the ASL-3 Security Standard.

units.context_stem: We will test for this checkpoint and, by the time we reach it, we will:
units.excerpt: share an update on our progress around that time;
units.paraphrase: An update on progress will be shared around the time the checkpoint is reached.

units.context_stem: We will test for this checkpoint and, by the time we reach it, we will:
units.excerpt: begin testing for the full Autonomous AI R&D Capability Threshold and any additional risks.
units.paraphrase: Testing for the full Autonomous AI R&D threshold and additional risks will begin at that time.

units.excerpt: We will also maintain a list of capabilities that we think require significant investigation and may require stronger safeguards than ASL-2 provides.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will maintain a list of capabilities warranting significant investigation and possibly stronger-than-ASL-2 safeguards.

units.excerpt: This group of capabilities could pose serious risks, but the exact Capability Threshold and the Required Safeguards are not clear at present.
units.paraphrase: These capabilities could pose serious risks, but the precise threshold and safeguards are not yet clear.

units.excerpt: These capabilities may warrant a higher standard of safeguards, such as the ASL-3 Security or Deployment Standard.
units.paraphrase: Such capabilities may warrant higher safeguards, such as ASL-3 Security or Deployment Standards.

units.excerpt: However, it is also possible that by the time these capabilities are reached, there will be evidence that such a standard is not necessary (for example, because of the potential use of similar capabilities for defensive purposes).
units.paraphrase: It is also possible that by the time these capabilities are reached, evidence will show the higher standard is unnecessary, e.g., due to defensive uses.

units.excerpt: Instead of prespecifying particular thresholds and safeguards today, we will conduct ongoing assessments of the risks with the goal of determining in a future iteration of this policy what the Capability Thresholds and Required Safeguards would be.
units.paraphrase: Rather than prespecifying thresholds now, ongoing risk assessments will inform future policy iterations defining these thresholds and safeguards.

units.excerpt: At present, we have identified one such capability:
units.paraphrase: One such capability has currently been identified.

units.excerpt: Cyber Operations: The ability to significantly enhance or automate sophisticated destructive cyber attacks, including but not limited to discovering novel zero-day exploit chains, developing complex malware, or orchestrating extensive hard-to-detect network intrusions.
units.paraphrase: Cyber Operations capability involves significantly enhancing or automating sophisticated destructive cyberattacks, such as zero-day exploit discovery, malware development, or extensive intrusions.

units.context_stem: Row: Cyber Operations; Column: Ongoing Assessment
units.excerpt: This will involve engaging with experts in cyber operations to assess the potential for frontier models to both enhance and mitigate cyber threats, and considering the implementation of tiered access controls or phased deployments for models with advanced cyber capabilities.
units.paraphrase: Ongoing assessment involves engaging cyber experts to evaluate both offensive and defensive potential, and considering tiered access or phased deployment for advanced cyber capabilities.

units.context_stem: Row: Cyber Operations; Column: Ongoing Assessment
units.excerpt: We will conduct either pre- or post-deployment testing, including specialized evaluations. We will document any salient results alongside our Capability Reports (see Section 3).
units.paraphrase: Pre- or post-deployment testing, including specialized evaluations, will be conducted, and salient results documented with Capability Reports.

units.excerpt: We hope to publish updates approximately every 6 months.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic hopes to publish updates roughly every six months.

units.excerpt: We recognize the potential risks of highly persuasive AI models. While we are actively consulting experts, we believe this capability is not yet sufficiently understood to include in our current commitments.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic recognizes risks from highly persuasive AI models but considers the capability not yet well enough understood for current commitments, despite ongoing expert consultation.

units.excerpt: Overall, our decision to prioritize the capabilities in the two tables above is based on commissioned research reports, discussions with domain experts, input from expert forecasters, public research, conversations with other industry actors through the Frontier Model Forum, and internal discussions.
units.paraphrase: Prioritization of the listed capabilities draws on commissioned research, expert discussions, forecaster input, public research, Frontier Model Forum conversations, and internal discussions.

units.excerpt: As the field evolves and our understanding deepens, we remain committed to refining our approach.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic remains committed to refining its approach as the field evolves and understanding deepens.

units.excerpt: We will routinely test models to determine whether their capabilities fall sufficiently far below the Capability Thresholds such that we are confident that the ASL-2 Standard remains appropriate.
units.paraphrase: Routine testing checks whether models remain sufficiently below thresholds such that ASL-2 remains appropriate.

units.excerpt: We will first conduct preliminary assessments (on both new and existing models, as needed) to determine whether a more comprehensive evaluation is needed.
units.paraphrase: Preliminary assessments on new and existing models, as needed, determine whether comprehensive evaluation is warranted.

units.excerpt: The purpose of this preliminary assessment is to identify whether the model is notably more capable than the last model that underwent a comprehensive assessment.
units.paraphrase: The preliminary assessment's purpose is to check whether the model is notably more capable than the last comprehensively assessed model.

units.excerpt: The term "notably more capable" is operationalized as at least one of the following:
units.paraphrase: "Notably more capable" is defined as meeting at least one of the following criteria.

units.context_stem: The term "notably more capable" is operationalized as at least one of the following:
units.excerpt: The model is notably more performant on automated tests in risk-relevant domains (defined as 4x or more in Effective Compute).
units.paraphrase: One criterion for "notably more capable" is a 4x or greater increase in Effective Compute-equivalent performance on risk-relevant automated tests.

units.context_stem: The term "notably more capable" is operationalized as at least one of the following:
units.excerpt: Six months' worth of finetuning and other capability elicitation methods have accumulated. This is measured in calendar time, since we do not yet have a metric to estimate the impact of these improvements more precisely.
units.paraphrase: Another criterion is the accumulation of six months of finetuning and elicitation methods, measured in calendar time absent a more precise metric.

units.excerpt: In addition, the Responsible Scaling Officer may in their discretion determine that a comprehensive assessment is warranted.
units.paraphrase: The Responsible Scaling Officer may also determine at their discretion that comprehensive assessment is warranted.

units.excerpt: If a new or existing model is below the "notably more capable" standard, no further testing is necessary.
units.paraphrase: No further testing is needed if the model is below the "notably more capable" standard.

units.excerpt: For models requiring comprehensive testing, we will assess whether the model is unlikely to reach any relevant Capability Thresholds absent surprising advances in widely accessible post-training enhancements.
units.paraphrase: Comprehensive testing assesses whether a model is unlikely to reach relevant thresholds absent surprising widely-accessible post-training advances.

units.excerpt: To make the required showing, we will need to satisfy the following criteria:
units.paraphrase: Satisfying the required showing requires meeting the following criteria.

units.context_stem: To make the required showing, we will need to satisfy the following criteria:
units.excerpt: Threat model mapping: For each capability threshold, make a compelling case that we have mapped out the most likely and consequential threat models: combinations of actors (if relevant), attack pathways, model capability bottlenecks, and types of harms.
units.paraphrase: Threat model mapping requires a compelling case identifying the most likely and consequential threat models across actors, attack pathways, capability bottlenecks, and harm types.

units.excerpt: We also make a compelling case that there does not exist a threat model that we are not evaluating that represents a substantial amount of risk.
units.paraphrase: A compelling case is also made that no unevaluated threat model represents substantial risk.

units.context_stem: To make the required showing, we will need to satisfy the following criteria:
units.excerpt: Evaluations: Design and run empirical tests that provide strong evidence that the model does not have the requisite skills; explain why the tests yielded such results; and check at test time that the results are attributable to the model's capabilities rather than issues with the test design.
units.paraphrase: Evaluations require empirical tests providing strong evidence of lacking skills, explanation of results, and verification that results reflect capability rather than test design flaws.

units.excerpt: Findings from partner organizations and external evaluations of our models (or similar models) should also be incorporated into the final assessment, when available.
units.paraphrase: Findings from partner organizations and external evaluations should be incorporated into the final assessment when available.

units.context_stem: To make the required showing, we will need to satisfy the following criteria:
units.excerpt: Elicitation: Demonstrate that, when given enough resources to extrapolate to realistic attackers, researchers cannot elicit sufficiently useful results from the model on the relevant tasks.
units.paraphrase: Elicitation requires demonstrating that researchers, given resources approximating realistic attackers, cannot elicit sufficiently useful results on relevant tasks.

units.excerpt: We should assume that jailbreaks and model weight theft are possibilities, and therefore perform testing on models without safety mechanisms (such as harmlessness training) that could obscure these capabilities.
units.paraphrase: Testing should assume jailbreaks and weight theft are possible, and should be performed on models without safety mechanisms that could mask capabilities.

units.excerpt: We will also consider the possible performance increase from using resources that a realistic attacker would have access to, such as scaffolding, finetuning, and expert prompting.
units.paraphrase: Possible performance gains from attacker-accessible resources like scaffolding, finetuning, and expert prompting will also be considered.

units.excerpt: At minimum, we will perform basic finetuning for instruction following, tool use, minimizing refusal rates.
units.paraphrase: At minimum, basic finetuning will be performed for instruction following, tool use, and minimizing refusal rates.

units.excerpt: "Effective Compute" is a scaling-trend-based metric that accounts for both FLOPs and algorithmic improvements. An Effective Compute increase of K represents a performance improvement from a pretrained model on relevant task(s) equivalent to scaling up the baseline model's training compute by a factor of K.
units.paraphrase: Effective Compute is a scaling-trend metric combining FLOPs and algorithmic improvements, where an increase of K equates to a Kx training-compute scale-up in performance terms.

units.excerpt: We plan to track Effective Compute during pretraining on a weighted aggregation of datasets relevant to our Capability Thresholds (e.g., coding and science).
units.paraphrase: Effective Compute will be tracked during pretraining using a weighted aggregation of threshold-relevant datasets such as coding and science.

units.excerpt: This is, however, an open research question, and we will explore different possible methods.
units.paraphrase: Tracking Effective Compute remains an open research question, with different methods to be explored.

units.excerpt: More generally, the Effective Compute concept is fairly new, and we may replace it with another metric in a similar spirit in the future.
units.paraphrase: The Effective Compute concept is fairly new and may be replaced by a similar metric in the future.

units.excerpt: This is a broad category, including techniques like improved prompting and agent scaffolding.
units.paraphrase: The category is broad, including techniques such as improved prompting and agent scaffolding.

units.excerpt: Exploring ways to integrate these types of improvements into an overall metric is an ongoing area of research.
units.paraphrase: Integrating these improvements into an overall metric remains an ongoing research area.

units.excerpt: By "widely accessible," we mean techniques that are available to a moderately resourced group (i.e., do not involve setting up large amounts of custom infrastructure or using confidential information).
units.paraphrase: "Widely accessible" refers to techniques available to moderately resourced groups without extensive custom infrastructure or confidential information.

units.excerpt: We include headroom to account for the possibility that the model is either modified via one of our own finetuning products or stolen in the months following testing, and used to create a model that has reached a Capability Threshold.
units.paraphrase: Headroom is included to account for the model being modified via finetuning products or stolen after testing and used to reach a Capability Threshold.

units.excerpt: That said, estimating these future effects is very difficult given the state of research today.
units.paraphrase: Estimating these future effects is currently very difficult given the state of research.

units.context_stem: To make the required showing, we will need to satisfy the following criteria:
units.excerpt: Forecasting: Make informal forecasts about the likelihood that further training and elicitation will improve test results between the time of testing and the next expected round of comprehensive testing.
units.paraphrase: Forecasting requires informal forecasts of whether further training and elicitation will improve results before the next comprehensive testing round.

units.excerpt: This testing and the subsequent capability decision should ideally be concluded within about a month of reaching the "notably more capable" threshold.
units.paraphrase: Testing and the capability decision should ideally conclude within about a month of reaching the "notably more capable" threshold.

units.excerpt: If, after the comprehensive testing, we determine that the model is sufficiently below the relevant Capability Thresholds, then we will continue to apply the ASL-2 Standard.
units.paraphrase: If comprehensive testing shows the model is sufficiently below thresholds, ASL-2 continues to apply.

units.excerpt: The process for making such a determination is as follows:
units.paraphrase: The following steps describe the process for making that determination.

units.context_stem: The process for making such a determination is as follows:
units.excerpt: First, we will compile a Capability Report that documents the findings from the comprehensive assessment, makes an affirmative case for why the Capability Threshold is sufficiently far away, and advances recommendations on deployment decisions.
units.paraphrase: A Capability Report is compiled documenting findings, making the case for distance from the threshold, and recommending deployment decisions.

units.context_stem: The process for making such a determination is as follows:
units.excerpt: The report will be escalated to the CEO and the Responsible Scaling Officer, who will (1) make the ultimate determination as to whether we have sufficiently established that we are unlikely to reach the Capability Threshold and (2) decide any deployment-related issues.
units.paraphrase: The report is escalated to the CEO and RSO, who make the ultimate determination on threshold likelihood and decide deployment issues.

units.context_stem: The process for making such a determination is as follows:
units.excerpt: In general, as noted in Sections 7.1.4 and 7.2.2, we will solicit both internal and external expert feedback on the report as well as the CEO and RSO's conclusions to inform future refinements to our methodology.
units.paraphrase: Internal and external expert feedback on the report and conclusions is generally solicited to inform methodological refinements.

units.context_stem: The process for making such a determination is as follows:
units.excerpt: For high-stakes issues, however, the CEO and RSO will likely solicit internal and external feedback on the report prior to making any decisions.
units.paraphrase: For high-stakes issues, the CEO and RSO will likely solicit feedback before making decisions.

units.context_stem: The process for making such a determination is as follows:
units.excerpt: If the CEO and RSO decide to proceed with deployment, they will share their decision–as well as the underlying Capability Report, internal feedback, and any external feedback–with the Board of Directors and the Long-Term Benefit Trust before moving forward.
units.paraphrase: If deployment is approved, the CEO and RSO will share the decision, Capability Report, and feedback with the Board and Long-Term Benefit Trust before proceeding.

units.excerpt: If, however, we determine we are unable to make the required showing, we will act as though the model has surpassed the Capability Threshold.
units.paraphrase: If the required showing cannot be made, the model is treated as having surpassed the threshold.

units.excerpt: This means that we will (1) upgrade to the ASL-3 Required Safeguards (see Section 4) and (2) conduct follow-up a capability assessment to confirm that the ASL-4 Standard is not necessary (see Section 5).
units.paraphrase: This triggers an upgrade to ASL-3 Required Safeguards and a follow-up capability assessment confirming ASL-4 is unnecessary.

units.excerpt: To determine whether the measures we have adopted satisfy the ASL-3 Required Safeguards, we will conduct a safeguards assessment.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will conduct a safeguards assessment to check whether its measures meet the ASL-3 Required Safeguards.

units.excerpt: As noted, the Required Safeguards for each Capability Threshold are specified in Section 2.
units.paraphrase: The Required Safeguards for each Capability Threshold appear in Section 2.

units.excerpt: We will document our implementation of the Required Safeguards in a Safeguards Report.
units.paraphrase: Implementation of the Required Safeguards will be documented in a Safeguards Report.

units.excerpt: Currently, these will be informal estimates of (1) the extent to which widely available elicitation techniques may improve and (2) how the model will perform on the same tasks when the next round of testing begins.
units.paraphrase: For now, forecasts will be informal estimates covering elicitation technique improvement and future task performance.

units.excerpt: As these are open research questions, we will aim to improve these forecasts over time so that they can be relied upon for risk judgments.
units.paraphrase: Because these are open research questions, forecasts will be improved over time to support risk judgments.

units.excerpt: In the case where the capability assessment shows a model is just barely below the threshold, the Responsible Scaling Officer may choose to limit further training to some amount less than the default 4x Effective Compute increase until ASL-3 measures are in place, in order to limit risk.
units.paraphrase: If a model is just barely below the threshold, the Responsible Scaling Officer may cap further training below the default 4x Effective Compute increase until ASL-3 measures are ready.

units.excerpt: There may be a substantial period during which models are not demonstrably close to the Capability Threshold, but we nevertheless are unable to rule out the risk to our satisfaction, and thus choose to implement the Required Safeguards.
units.paraphrase: Even when models are not clearly close to the Capability Threshold, Anthropic may implement Required Safeguards if it cannot rule out the risk to its satisfaction.

units.excerpt: When a model must meet the ASL-3 Deployment Standard, we will evaluate whether the measures we have implemented make us robust to persistent attempts to misuse the capability in question.
units.paraphrase: When the ASL-3 Deployment Standard applies, Anthropic will evaluate whether its measures make it robust to persistent misuse attempts.

units.excerpt: To make the required showing, we will need to satisfy the following criteria:
units.paraphrase: Lead-in stating that several criteria must be satisfied to demonstrate the standard is met.

units.context_stem: To make the required showing, we will need to satisfy the following criteria:
units.excerpt: Threat modeling: Make a compelling case that the set of threats and the vectors through which an adversary could catastrophically misuse the deployed system have been sufficiently mapped out, and will commit to revising as necessary over time.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic must convincingly show threats and misuse vectors have been mapped and commit to revising the threat model over time.

units.context_stem: To make the required showing, we will need to satisfy the following criteria:
units.excerpt: Defense in depth: Use a "defense in depth" approach by building a series of defensive layers, each designed to catch misuse attempts that might pass through previous barriers.
units.paraphrase: A layered defensive approach must be used, with each layer designed to catch misuse attempts that pass earlier layers.

units.excerpt: As an example, this might entail achieving a high overall recall rate using harm refusal techniques. This is an area of active research, and new technologies may be added when ready.
units.paraphrase: An example is high recall via harm refusal techniques; this is active research and new technologies may be added later.

units.context_stem: To make the required showing, we will need to satisfy the following criteria:
units.excerpt: Red-teaming: Conduct red-teaming that demonstrates that threat actors with realistic access levels and resources are highly unlikely to be able to consistently elicit information from any generally accessible systems that greatly increases their ability to cause catastrophic harm relative to other available tools.
units.paraphrase: Red-teaming must show realistic threat actors are highly unlikely to extract catastrophic-harm-enabling information beyond what other tools already provide.

units.context_stem: To make the required showing, we will need to satisfy the following criteria:
units.excerpt: Rapid remediation: Show that any compromises of the deployed system, such as jailbreaks or other attack pathways, will be identified and remediated promptly enough to prevent the overall system from meaningfully increasing an adversary's ability to cause catastrophic harm.
units.paraphrase: Must demonstrate compromises like jailbreaks will be identified and fixed quickly enough to prevent meaningful uplift to adversaries.

units.excerpt: Example techniques could include rapid vulnerability patching, the ability to escalate to law enforcement when appropriate, and any necessary retention of logs for these activities.
units.paraphrase: Example techniques include rapid patching, law enforcement escalation, and log retention.

units.context_stem: To make the required showing, we will need to satisfy the following criteria:
units.excerpt: Monitoring: Prespecify empirical evidence that would show the system is operating within the accepted risk range and define a process for reviewing the system's performance on a reasonable cadence.
units.paraphrase: Must prespecify evidence showing acceptable risk range operation and define a periodic review process.

units.excerpt: Process examples include monitoring responses to jailbreak bounties, doing historical analysis or background monitoring, and any necessary retention of logs for these activities.
units.paraphrase: Example processes include jailbreak bounty monitoring, historical/background analysis, and log retention.

units.context_stem: To make the required showing, we will need to satisfy the following criteria:
units.excerpt: Trusted users: Establish criteria for determining when it may be appropriate to share a version of the model with reduced safeguards with trusted users. In addition, demonstrate that an alternative set of controls will provide equivalent levels of assurance.
units.paraphrase: Must set criteria for sharing reduced-safeguard versions with trusted users and show alternative controls give equivalent assurance.

units.excerpt: This could include a sufficient combination of user vetting, secure access controls, monitoring, log retention, and incident response protocols.
units.paraphrase: Could include user vetting, secure access controls, monitoring, log retention, and incident response protocols.

units.context_stem: To make the required showing, we will need to satisfy the following criteria:
units.excerpt: Third-party environments: Document how all relevant models will meet the criteria above, even if they are deployed in a third-party partner's environment that may have a different set of safeguards.
units.paraphrase: Must document how models meet the above criteria even when deployed in third-party environments with different safeguards.

units.excerpt: When a model must meet the ASL-3 Security Standard, we will evaluate whether the measures we have implemented make us highly protected against most attackers' attempts at stealing model weights.
units.paraphrase: When the ASL-3 Security Standard applies, Anthropic will evaluate whether it is highly protected against most weight-theft attempts.

units.excerpt: This criterion does not attempt to specify the exact red-teaming protocol (e.g., number of hours, level of access, or pass-fail criteria). Setting a principled pass-fail threshold will depend on other factors, such as the quality of our monitoring and ability to respond to jailbreaks rapidly.
units.paraphrase: The red-teaming criterion leaves protocol details unspecified; the pass-fail threshold depends on monitoring quality and rapid response ability.

units.excerpt: Due to the likely ease of bypassing or removing safeguards via fine-tuning, it may be difficult or impossible for these red-teaming tests to pass if weights are released or if unmoderated fine-tuning access is provided to untrusted users.
units.paraphrase: Red-teaming tests may be very hard to pass if weights are released or unmoderated fine-tuning access is given to untrusted users, since safeguards can be easily bypassed via fine-tuning.

units.excerpt: We consider the following groups in scope: hacktivists, criminal hacker groups, organized cybercrime groups, terrorist organizations, corporate espionage teams, internal employees, and state-sponsored programs that use broad-based and non-targeted techniques (i.e., not novel attack chains).
units.paraphrase: In-scope threat actors include hacktivists, criminal groups, terrorists, corporate espionage teams, insiders, and state-sponsored programs using non-targeted techniques.

units.excerpt: The following groups are out of scope for the ASL-3 Security Standard because further testing (as discussed below) should confirm that the model would not meaningfully increase their ability to do harm:
units.paraphrase: Lead-in identifying groups excluded from ASL-3 Security Standard scope, pending further testing confirmation.

units.context_stem: Groups out of scope for ASL-3 Security Standard
units.excerpt: state-sponsored programs that specifically target us (e.g., through novel attack chains or insider compromise) and a small number (~10) of non-state actors with state-level resourcing or backing that are capable of developing novel attack chains that utilize 0-day attacks.
units.paraphrase: Out-of-scope actors are state programs specifically targeting Anthropic and roughly ten non-state actors with state-level resources capable of novel zero-day attack chains.

units.excerpt: To make the required showing, we will need to satisfy the following criteria:
units.paraphrase: Lead-in stating criteria to be satisfied for the ASL-3 Security Standard.

units.context_stem: To make the required showing, we will need to satisfy the following criteria:
units.excerpt: Threat modeling: Follow risk governance best practices, such as use of the MITRE ATT&CK Framework to establish the relationship between the identified threats, sensitive assets, attack vectors and, in doing so, sufficiently capture the resulting risks that must be addressed to protect model weights from theft attempts.
units.paraphrase: Must follow risk governance best practices such as MITRE ATT&CK to map threats, assets, and vectors and capture the risks to weight security.

units.excerpt: As part of this requirement, we should specify our plans for revising the resulting threat model over time.
units.paraphrase: Must also specify plans for revising the threat model over time.

units.context_stem: To make the required showing, we will need to satisfy the following criteria:
units.excerpt: Security frameworks: Align to and, as needed, extend industry-standard security frameworks for addressing identified risks, such as disclosure of sensitive information, tampering with accounts and assets, and unauthorized elevation of privileges with the appropriate controls.
units.paraphrase: Must align with and extend industry-standard security frameworks to address risks like data disclosure, tampering, and privilege escalation.

units.excerpt: This includes:
units.paraphrase: Lead-in to sub-items of the security frameworks criterion.

units.context_stem: Security frameworks: Align to and extend industry-standard security frameworks. This includes:
units.excerpt: Perimeters and access controls: Building strong perimeters and access controls around sensitive assets to ensure AI models and critical systems are protected from unauthorized access.
units.paraphrase: Sub-criterion requiring strong perimeters and access controls protecting AI models and critical systems from unauthorized access.

units.excerpt: We expect this will include a combination of physical security, encryption, cloud security, infrastructure policy, access management, and weight access minimization and monitoring.
units.paraphrase: Expected components include physical security, encryption, cloud security, infrastructure policy, access management, and weight access minimization/monitoring.

units.context_stem: Security frameworks: Align to and extend industry-standard security frameworks. This includes:
units.excerpt: Lifecycle security: Securing links in the chain of systems and software used to develop models, to prevent compromised components from being introduced and to ensure only trusted code and hardware is used.
units.paraphrase: Sub-criterion requiring securing of the development supply chain against compromised components and untrusted code/hardware.

units.excerpt: We expect this will include a combination of software inventory, supply chain security, artifact integrity, binary authorization, hardware procurement, and secure research development lifecycle.
units.paraphrase: Expected components include software inventory, supply chain security, artifact integrity, binary authorization, hardware procurement, and secure R&D lifecycle.

units.context_stem: Security frameworks: Align to and extend industry-standard security frameworks. This includes:
units.excerpt: Monitoring: Proactively identifying and mitigating threats through ongoing and effective monitoring, testing for vulnerabilities, and laying traps for potential attackers.
units.paraphrase: Sub-criterion requiring proactive threat identification/mitigation via monitoring, vulnerability testing, and attacker traps.

units.excerpt: We expect this will include a combination of endpoint patching, product security testing, log management, asset monitoring, and intruder deception techniques.
units.paraphrase: Expected components include endpoint patching, product security testing, log management, asset monitoring, and intruder deception techniques.

units.context_stem: Security frameworks: Align to and extend industry-standard security frameworks. This includes:
units.excerpt: Resourcing: Investing sufficient resources in security.
units.paraphrase: Sub-criterion requiring sufficient investment of resources in security.

units.excerpt: We expect meeting this standard of security to require roughly 5-10% of employees being dedicated to security and security-adjacent work.
units.paraphrase: Meeting the security standard is expected to require about 5-10% of employees dedicated to security-related work.

units.context_stem: Security frameworks: Align to and extend industry-standard security frameworks. This includes:
units.excerpt: Existing guidance: Aligning where appropriate with existing guidance on securing model weights, including Securing AI Model Weights, Preventing Theft and Misuse of Frontier Models (2024); security recommendations like Deploying AI Systems Securely (CISA/NSA/FBI/ASD/CCCS/GCSB /GCHQ), ISO 42001, CSA's AI Safety Initiative, and CoSAI; and standards frameworks like SSDF, SOC 2, NIST 800-53.
units.paraphrase: Sub-criterion requiring alignment with named existing guidance and standards frameworks on securing model weights.

units.excerpt: We will implement robust insider risk controls to mitigate most insider risk, but consider mitigating risks from highly sophisticated state-compromised insiders to be out of scope for ASL-3.
units.paraphrase: Robust insider risk controls will be implemented, but mitigating highly sophisticated state-compromised insider risks is out of scope for ASL-3.

units.excerpt: We are committed to further enhancing these protections as a part of our ASL-4 preparations.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic commits to further enhancing insider risk protections as part of ASL-4 preparations.

units.context_stem: To make the required showing, we will need to satisfy the following criteria:
units.excerpt: Audits: Develop plans to (1) audit and assess the design and implementation of the security program and (2) share these findings (and updates on any remediation efforts) with management on an appropriate cadence.
units.paraphrase: Must develop plans to audit the security program and share findings and remediation updates with management periodically.

units.excerpt: We expect this to include independent validation of threat modeling and risk assessment results; a sampling-based audit of the operating effectiveness of the defined controls; periodic, broadly scoped, and independent testing with expert red-teamers who are industry-renowned and have been recognized in competitive challenges.
units.paraphrase: Expected audit elements include independent threat model/risk validation, sampling-based control audits, and periodic independent red-team testing by renowned experts.

units.context_stem: To make the required showing, we will need to satisfy the following criteria:
units.excerpt: Third-party environments: Document how all relevant models will meet the criteria above, even if they are deployed in a third-party partner's environment that may have a different set of safeguards.
units.paraphrase: Must document how models meet the above criteria even in third-party environments with different safeguards.

units.excerpt: If, after the evaluations above, we determine that we have met the ASL-3 Required Safeguards, then we may proceed with deploying and training models above the Capability Threshold, provided we have also conducted a follow-up capability assessment.
units.paraphrase: If the ASL-3 Required Safeguards are determined to be met, deployment and training above the Capability Threshold may proceed, provided a follow-up capability assessment is conducted.

units.excerpt: The process for determining whether we have met the ASL-3 Required Safeguards is as follows:
units.paraphrase: Lead-in introducing the process for determining whether the Required Safeguards have been met.

units.context_stem: The process for determining whether we have met the ASL-3 Required Safeguards is as follows:
units.excerpt: First, we will compile a Safeguards Report for each Required Safeguard that documents our implementation of the measures above, makes an affirmative case for why we have satisfied them, and advances recommendations on deployment decisions.
units.paraphrase: A Safeguards Report will first be compiled for each Required Safeguard, documenting implementation, making a case for satisfaction, and recommending deployment decisions.

units.context_stem: The process for determining whether we have met the ASL-3 Required Safeguards is as follows:
units.excerpt: The Safeguards Report(s) will be escalated to the CEO and the Responsible Scaling Officer, who will (1) make the ultimate determination as to whether we have satisfied the Required Safeguards and (2) decide any deployment-related issues.
units.paraphrase: The Safeguards Report will go to the CEO and RSO, who make the final determination of compliance and decide deployment issues.

units.context_stem: The process for determining whether we have met the ASL-3 Required Safeguards is as follows:
units.excerpt: In general, as noted in Sections 7.1.4 and 7.2.2, we will solicit both internal and external expert feedback on the report as well as the CEO and RSO's conclusions to inform future refinements to our methodology.
units.paraphrase: Internal and external expert feedback will generally be solicited on the report and conclusions to inform future methodology refinements.

units.excerpt: For high-stakes issues, however, the CEO and RSO will likely solicit internal and external feedback on the report prior to making any decisions.
units.paraphrase: For high-stakes issues, feedback will likely be solicited before decisions are made.

units.context_stem: The process for determining whether we have met the ASL-3 Required Safeguards is as follows:
units.excerpt: If the CEO and RSO decide to proceed with deployment and training, they will share their decision–as well as the underlying Safeguards Report, internal feedback, and any external feedback–with the Board of Directors and the Long-Term Benefit Trust before moving forward.
units.paraphrase: If proceeding with deployment/training, the CEO and RSO will share the decision and supporting materials with the Board and Long-Term Benefit Trust first.

units.context_stem: The process for determining whether we have met the ASL-3 Required Safeguards is as follows:
units.excerpt: After the ASL-3 Required Safeguards are approved, they will be revisited and re-approved at least annually to re-affirm their suitability and sound implementation.
units.paraphrase: Once approved, the Required Safeguards will be reviewed and re-approved at least once a year.

units.excerpt: If, however, we are unable to make the showing required above, we will restrict model deployment and further scaling.
units.paraphrase: If the required showing cannot be made, model deployment and further scaling will be restricted.

units.excerpt: In parallel with upgrading a model to the Required Safeguards, we will (1) update this policy to include any additional Capability Thresholds for which the Required Safeguards would be insufficient; and (2) conduct a follow-up capability assessment to determine that the model's capabilities fall sufficiently far away from those Capability Thresholds, following the procedures outlined in Section 3.
units.paraphrase: While upgrading a model to the Required Safeguards, the policy will be updated with any additional insufficient Capability Thresholds and a follow-up capability assessment will confirm sufficient distance from those thresholds, per Section 3 procedures.

units.excerpt: To summarize the commitments and procedures outlined above, we may deploy or store a model if either of the following criteria are met: (1) the model's capabilities are sufficiently far away from the existing Capability Thresholds, making the current ASL-2 Standard appropriate;
units.paraphrase: Deployment or storage may continue if the model's capabilities are sufficiently far from existing Capability Thresholds, keeping the ASL-2 Standard appropriate.

units.context_stem: we may deploy or store a model if either of the following criteria are met:
units.excerpt: or (2) the model's capabilities have surpassed the existing Capabilities Threshold, but we have implemented the ASL-3 Required Safeguards and confirmed that the model is sufficiently far away from the next set of Capability Thresholds as to make the model ASL-3 Standard appropriate.
units.paraphrase: Alternatively, deployment/storage may continue if capabilities exceed the existing threshold but ASL-3 Required Safeguards are implemented and sufficient distance from the next thresholds is confirmed.

units.excerpt: We may also continue to train more capable models, conducting preliminary and comprehensive assessments as before.
units.paraphrase: More capable models may continue to be trained, with preliminary and comprehensive assessments conducted as before.

units.excerpt: In any scenario where we determine that a model requires ASL-3 Required Safeguards but we are unable to implement them immediately, we will act promptly to reduce interim risk to acceptable levels until the ASL-3 Required Safeguards are in place:
units.paraphrase: If ASL-3 Required Safeguards are needed but cannot be implemented immediately, prompt action will reduce interim risk until the safeguards are ready.

units.context_stem: we will act promptly to reduce interim risk to acceptable levels until the ASL-3 Required Safeguards are in place:
units.excerpt: Interim measures: The CEO and Responsible Scaling Officer may approve the use of interim measures that provide the same level of assurance as the relevant ASL-3 Standard but are faster or simpler to implement.
units.paraphrase: The CEO and RSO may approve interim measures giving equivalent assurance to the ASL-3 Standard but quicker or simpler to implement.

units.excerpt: In the deployment context, such measures might include blocking model responses, downgrading to a less-capable model in a particular domain, or increasing the sensitivity of automated monitoring.
units.paraphrase: Deployment-context interim measures might include blocking responses, downgrading models in a domain, or increasing monitoring sensitivity.

units.excerpt: In the security context, an example of such a measure would be storing the model weights in a single-purpose, isolated network that meets the ASL-3 Standard.
units.paraphrase: In the security context, an example measure is storing weights in an isolated single-purpose network meeting the ASL-3 Standard.

units.excerpt: In either case, the CEO and Responsible Scaling Officer will share their plan with the Board of Directors and the Long-Term Benefit Trust.
units.paraphrase: Either way, the CEO and RSO will share the interim measures plan with the Board and Long-Term Benefit Trust.

units.context_stem: we will act promptly to reduce interim risk to acceptable levels until the ASL-3 Required Safeguards are in place:
units.excerpt: Stronger restrictions: In the unlikely event that we cannot implement interim measures to adequately mitigate risk, we will impose stronger restrictions.
units.paraphrase: If interim measures cannot adequately mitigate risk, stronger restrictions will be imposed.

units.excerpt: In the deployment context, we will de-deploy the model and replace it with a model that falls below the Capability Threshold. Once the ASL-3 Deployment Standard can be met, the model may be re-deployed.
units.paraphrase: In deployment, the model will be withdrawn and replaced by one below the Capability Threshold, with re-deployment possible once the ASL-3 Deployment Standard is met.

units.excerpt: In the security context, we will delete model weights. Given the availability of interim deployment and security protections, however, stronger restrictions should rarely be necessary.
units.paraphrase: In the security context, model weights will be deleted, though stronger restrictions should rarely be needed given available interim protections.

units.context_stem: we will act promptly to reduce interim risk to acceptable levels until the ASL-3 Required Safeguards are in place:
units.excerpt: Monitoring pretraining: We will not train models with comparable or greater capabilities to the one that requires the ASL-3 Security Standard.
units.paraphrase: Models with comparable or greater capabilities to the one requiring the ASL-3 Security Standard will not be trained.

units.excerpt: This is achieved by monitoring the capabilities of the model in pretraining and comparing them against the given model.
units.paraphrase: This is done by monitoring pretraining model capabilities and comparing them to the reference model.

units.excerpt: If the pretraining model's capabilities are comparable or greater, we will pause training until we have implemented the ASL-3 Security Standard and established it is sufficient for the model.
units.paraphrase: If pretraining capabilities are comparable or greater, training will pause until the ASL-3 Security Standard is implemented and confirmed sufficient.

units.excerpt: We will set expectations with internal stakeholders about the potential for such pauses.
units.paraphrase: Internal stakeholders will be given expectations about the possibility of such training pauses.

units.excerpt: When choosing amongst options that satisfy the safety criteria, we will implement whichever interim safeguards minimize changes to customer experience.
units.paraphrase: Among safety-satisfying options, the interim safeguards chosen will be those minimizing customer experience changes.

units.excerpt: We consider implementation of the ASL-3 Security Standard alone sufficient to continue training, regardless of whether the ASL-3 Deployment Standard is satisfied.
units.paraphrase: Implementing the ASL-3 Security Standard alone is considered sufficient to continue training, irrespective of the Deployment Standard.

units.excerpt: "Comparable or greater capabilities" is operationalized as 1x or more in Effective Compute.
units.paraphrase: The term "comparable or greater capabilities" is defined as 1x or more Effective Compute.

units.excerpt: We will maintain the position of Responsible Scaling Officer, a designated member of staff who is responsible for reducing catastrophic risk, primarily by ensuring this policy is designed and implemented effectively.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic commits to maintaining a Responsible Scaling Officer role responsible for reducing catastrophic risk through effective policy implementation.

units.context_stem: The Responsible Scaling Officer's duties will include (but are not limited to):
units.excerpt: (1) as needed, proposing updates to this policy to the Board of Directors; (2) approving relevant model training or deployment decisions based on capability and safeguard assessments; (3) reviewing major contracts (i.e., deployment partnerships) for consistency with this policy;
