units.paraphrase: The RSO's duties include proposing policy updates, approving training/deployment decisions, and reviewing major contracts for policy consistency.

units.context_stem: The Responsible Scaling Officer's duties will include (but are not limited to):
units.excerpt: (4) overseeing implementation of this policy, including the allocation of sufficient resources; (5) receiving and addressing reports of potential instances of noncompliance; (6) promptly notifying the Board of Directors of any cases of noncompliance that pose material risk; and (7) making judgment calls on policy interpretation and application.
units.paraphrase: The RSO's duties also include overseeing implementation and resourcing, handling noncompliance reports, notifying the Board of material risk, and interpreting the policy.

units.excerpt: We will develop internal safety procedures for incident scenarios. Such scenarios include (1) pausing training in response to reaching Capability Thresholds; (2) responding to a security incident involving model weights; and (3) responding to severe jailbreaks or vulnerabilities in deployed models, including restricting access in safety emergencies that cannot otherwise be mitigated.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will create internal procedures for handling incidents such as pausing training, security breaches of model weights, and severe jailbreaks.

units.excerpt: We will run exercises to ensure our readiness for incident scenarios.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will conduct exercises to test readiness for incident scenarios.

units.excerpt: We will share summaries of Capability Reports and Safeguards Reports with Anthropic's regular-clearance staff, redacting any highly-sensitive information.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will share redacted summaries of Capability and Safeguards Reports with regular-clearance staff.

units.excerpt: We will share a minimally redacted version of these reports with a subset of staff, to help us surface relevant technical safety considerations.
units.paraphrase: A subset of staff will receive a minimally redacted version of the reports to help surface safety considerations.

units.excerpt: For each Capabilities or Safeguards Report, we will solicit feedback from internal teams with visibility into the relevant activities, with the aims of informing future refinements to our methodology and, in some circumstances, identifying weaknesses and informing the CEO and RSO's decisions.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will seek internal feedback on each Capabilities or Safeguards Report to refine methodology and inform decisions.

units.excerpt: We will maintain a process through which Anthropic staff may anonymously notify the Responsible Scaling Officer of any potential instances of noncompliance with this policy.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will maintain an anonymous reporting process for staff to notify the RSO of potential noncompliance.

units.excerpt: We will also establish a policy governing noncompliance reporting, which will (1) protect reporters from retaliation and (2) set forth a mechanism for escalating reports to one or more members of the Board of Directors in cases where the report relates to conduct of the Responsible Scaling Officer.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will establish a noncompliance reporting policy that protects reporters and provides escalation to the Board when the RSO is implicated.

units.excerpt: Further, we will track and investigate any reported or otherwise identified potential instances of noncompliance with this policy. Where reports are substantiated, we will take appropriate and proportional corrective action and document the same.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will track, investigate, and take documented corrective action on substantiated noncompliance instances.

units.excerpt: The Responsible Scaling Officer will regularly update the Board of Directors on substantial cases of noncompliance and overall trends.
units.paraphrase: The RSO will provide regular Board updates on substantial noncompliance cases and trends.

units.excerpt: In addition to noncompliance processes, we will (1) establish pathways for Anthropic staff to raise any issues related to this policy, including the overall risk levels of our models and implementation challenges; and (2) regularly review our compliance with this policy's procedural requirements.
units.paraphrase: Beyond noncompliance channels, Anthropic will create pathways for staff to raise policy concerns and will regularly review procedural compliance.

units.excerpt: Cases deemed to present minimal additional risk may be reported to the Board in quarterly summary reports.
units.paraphrase: Low-risk noncompliance cases may be reported via quarterly summaries instead of immediately.

units.excerpt: In cases where this policy is unintentionally ambiguous, we will act in accordance with the Responsible Scaling Officer or CEO's judgment, and aim to clarify the ambiguity in the next policy update.
units.paraphrase: Ambiguities will be resolved via RSO or CEO judgment, with clarification intended in the next update.

units.excerpt: We will not impose contractual non-disparagement obligations on employees, candidates, or former employees in a way that could impede or discourage them from publicly raising safety concerns about Anthropic.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will not use non-disparagement clauses to prevent staff from raising public safety concerns.

units.excerpt: If we offer agreements with a non-disparagement clause, that clause will not preclude raising safety concerns, nor will it preclude disclosure of the existence of that clause.
units.paraphrase: Any non-disparagement clauses offered will not block raising safety concerns or disclosing the clause's existence.

units.excerpt: Changes to this policy will be proposed by the CEO and the Responsible Scaling Officer and approved by the Board of Directors, in consultation with the Long-Term Benefit Trust.
units.paraphrase: Policy changes are proposed by the CEO and RSO and approved by the Board, in consultation with the Long-Term Benefit Trust.

units.excerpt: The current version of the RSP is accessible at www.anthropic.com/rsp. We will update the public version of the RSP before any changes take effect and record any differences from the prior draft in a change log.
units.paraphrase: The RSP is publicly accessible online, and updates will be published before taking effect with a change log documenting differences.

units.excerpt: It is possible at some point in the future that another actor in the frontier AI ecosystem will pass, or be on track to imminently pass, a Capability Threshold without implementing measures equivalent to the Required Safeguards such that their actions pose a serious risk for the world.
units.paraphrase: A future scenario could occur where another AI actor surpasses a Capability Threshold without equivalent safeguards, posing serious global risk.

units.excerpt: In such a scenario, because the incremental increase in risk attributable to us would be small, we might decide to lower the Required Safeguards.
units.paraphrase: In that scenario, Anthropic might lower Required Safeguards since its own incremental risk contribution would be small.

units.excerpt: If we take this measure, however, we will also acknowledge the overall level of risk posed by AI systems (including ours), and will invest significantly in making a case to the U.S. government for taking regulatory action to mitigate such risk to acceptable levels.
units.paraphrase: If safeguards are lowered under this scenario, Anthropic will acknowledge overall AI risk and advocate for U.S. government regulatory action.

units.section_heading: 7. Governance and Transparency / 7.2. Transparency and External Input
units.excerpt: We will publicly release key information related to the evaluation and deployment of our models (not including sensitive details).
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will publicly release key model evaluation and deployment information, excluding sensitive details.

units.section_heading: 7. Governance and Transparency / 7.2. Transparency and External Input
units.excerpt: These include summaries of related Capability and Safeguards reports when we deploy a model as well as plans for current and future comprehensive capability assessments and deployment and security safeguards.
units.paraphrase: Public disclosures include report summaries at deployment and plans for capability assessments and safeguards.

units.section_heading: 7. Governance and Transparency / 7.2. Transparency and External Input
units.excerpt: We will also periodically release information on internal reports of potential instances of non-compliance and other implementation challenges we encounter.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will periodically release information about noncompliance reports and implementation challenges.

units.section_heading: 7. Governance and Transparency / 7.2. Transparency and External Input
units.excerpt: We will solicit input from external experts in relevant domains in the process of developing and conducting capability and safeguards assessments.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will seek external expert input while developing and conducting capability and safeguards assessments.

units.section_heading: 7. Governance and Transparency / 7.2. Transparency and External Input
units.excerpt: We may also solicit external expert input prior to making final decisions on the capability and safeguards assessments.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic may also seek external input before finalizing capability and safeguards assessment decisions.

units.section_heading: 7. Governance and Transparency / 7.2. Transparency and External Input
units.excerpt: We will notify a relevant U.S. Government entity if a model requires stronger protections than the ASL-2 Standard.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will notify a relevant U.S. Government entity when a model requires stronger-than-ASL-2 protections.

units.section_heading: 7. Governance and Transparency / 7.2. Transparency and External Input
units.excerpt: On approximately an annual basis, we will commission a third-party review that assesses whether we adhered to this policy's main procedural commitments (we expect to iterate on the exact list since this has not been done before for RSPs).
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will commission an annual third-party review of procedural compliance with the policy, expecting to refine the review's scope over time.

units.section_heading: 7. Governance and Transparency / 7.2. Transparency and External Input
units.excerpt: This review will focus on procedural compliance, not substantive outcomes. We will also do such reviews internally on a more regular cadence.
units.paraphrase: The third-party review addresses procedure not outcomes, and similar reviews will also be done internally more frequently.

units.section_heading: 7. Governance and Transparency / 7.2. Transparency and External Input
units.excerpt: We currently expect that if we do not deploy the model publicly and instead proceed with training or limited deployments, we will likely instead share evaluation details with a relevant U.S. Government entity.
units.paraphrase: For non-public deployments, Anthropic expects to share evaluation details with a U.S. Government entity instead.

units.section_heading: 7. Governance and Transparency / 7.2. Transparency and External Input
units.excerpt: These will be posted to www.anthropic.com/rsp-updates. We anticipate providing updates at least every 6-12 months.
units.paraphrase: Updates will be posted online, anticipated at least every 6-12 months.

units.section_heading: 7. Governance and Transparency / 7.2. Transparency and External Input
units.excerpt: Where possible, we will include descriptions of the empirical evaluation results we believe would indicate that a model is no longer safe to store under the ASL-2 Standard.
units.paraphrase: Updates will where possible describe evaluation results indicating a model is no longer safe under ASL-2.

units.section_heading: 7. Governance and Transparency / 7.2. Transparency and External Input
units.excerpt: Our purpose in these updates is to provide sufficient detail to facilitate conversations about best practices for safeguards, capability evaluations, and elicitation.
units.paraphrase: The intent of these updates is to enable dialogue about best practices in safeguards and evaluation.

units.excerpt: Technical and operational standards for safely training and deploying frontier AI models. Higher ASLs correspond to stronger safety and security measures required for more capable models.
units.paraphrase: ASLs are standards for safe training/deployment, with higher levels requiring stronger safeguards for more capable models.

units.excerpt: The current default standard for all Anthropic models, including security measures, safety testing, and automated misuse detection.
units.paraphrase: ASL-2 is the baseline standard for all Anthropic models covering security, safety testing, and misuse detection.

units.excerpt: A higher level of safeguards required when a model cannot be certified as ASL-2 appropriate. It includes more stringent security and deployment measures designed to mitigate risks from more capable models.
units.paraphrase: ASL-3 applies when a model cannot be certified ASL-2 appropriate, requiring stricter security and deployment measures.

units.excerpt: A document attesting that a model is sufficiently far from each of the relevant Capability Thresholds, and therefore (still) appropriate for storing under an ASL-N Standard. It includes evaluation procedures, results, and other relevant evidence gathered around the time of testing.
units.paraphrase: A Capability Report is documentation showing a model remains sufficiently distant from Capability Thresholds, including evaluation details.

units.excerpt: Specific AI capabilities that, if reached, would require stronger safeguards than the current baseline ASL-N standard provides.
units.paraphrase: Capability Thresholds are specific capabilities that trigger the need for stronger safeguards.

units.excerpt: A scaling trend-based metric that accounts for both FLOPs and algorithmic improvements.
units.paraphrase: Effective Compute is a metric combining FLOPs and algorithmic improvements to track scaling trends.

units.excerpt: Empirical tests designed to provide early warning when a model is approaching a Capability Threshold. These tests are intended to trigger before a model actually reaches a dangerous capability.
units.paraphrase: Evaluations are tests meant to give early warning before a model reaches a dangerous capability.

units.excerpt: Floating-Point Operation(s). The amount of computation required to train or run a model. The number of FLOPs can be used as one indicator of a model's computational complexity and, indirectly, its potential capabilities.
units.paraphrase: FLOPs measure the computation required to train/run a model and indicate computational complexity and potential capability.

units.excerpt: Anthropic's Board of Directors approves the RSP and receives Capability Reports and Safeguards Reports. The LTBT is an external body that is consulted on policy changes and also provided with Capability Reports and Safeguards Reports. More details about the LTBT are available here.
units.paraphrase: The Board approves the RSP and receives reports; the LTBT is an external body consulted on policy changes and also given the reports.

units.excerpt: The standard of safety and security measures that must be implemented when a model reaches a Capability Threshold.
units.paraphrase: Required Safeguards are the safety/security measures mandated once a Capability Threshold is reached.

units.excerpt: A designated staff member responsible for reducing catastrophic risk, primarily by ensuring this policy is designed and implemented effectively. Their duties include reviewing policy updates, approving reports, overseeing implementation, and approving deployments.
units.paraphrase: The RSO is a staff member tasked with reducing catastrophic risk via policy design/implementation, report approval, and deployment sign-off.

units.excerpt: A document attesting that the implemented safeguards meet an ASL-N Standard. It details the design and planned implementation of safeguards, and evidence to demonstrate their expected effectiveness.
units.paraphrase: A Safeguards Report documents that implemented safeguards meet an ASL-N standard with supporting evidence.

units.locator: App B / ASL-2 Deployment Standard / item 1
units.excerpt: Acceptable use policies and model cards: Publication of model cards for significant new models describing capabilities, limitations, evaluations, and intended use cases.
units.paraphrase: ASL-2 deployment requires publishing model cards describing capabilities, limitations, evaluations, and use cases for significant new models.

units.locator: App B / ASL-2 Deployment Standard / item 1
units.excerpt: Enforcement of a Usage Policy that restricts, at a minimum, catastrophic and high harm use cases, including using the model to generate content that could cause severe risks to the continued existence of humankind, or direct and severe harm to individuals.
units.paraphrase: ASL-2 requires enforcing a Usage Policy prohibiting at minimum catastrophic and high-harm use cases.

units.locator: App B / ASL-2 Deployment Standard / item 2
units.excerpt: Harmlessness training and automated detection: Training models to refuse requests to aid in causing harm, such as with Constitutional AI or other improved techniques, and the use of model enhanced trust and safety detection and enforcement.
units.paraphrase: ASL-2 requires harmlessness training (e.g., Constitutional AI) and model-enhanced trust and safety detection/enforcement.

units.locator: App B / ASL-2 Deployment Standard / item 3
units.excerpt: Fine-tuning protections: In finetuning products, data is filtered for harmfulness, and models are subject to automated evaluation to check harmlessness features are not degraded.
units.paraphrase: Finetuning products must filter harmful data and undergo automated checks that harmlessness features remain intact.

units.locator: App B / ASL-2 Deployment Standard / item 3
units.excerpt: There are a very limited number of use cases where this tooling is disabled. These are negotiated on a case by case basis and considered only for extremely low risk use cases that involve company personnel.
units.paraphrase: A very limited number of low-risk, personnel-only use cases may disable this tooling, negotiated case by case.

units.locator: App B / ASL-2 Deployment Standard / item 4
units.excerpt: Vulnerability reporting channels: Clearly indicated paths within the product for users to report harmful or dangerous model outputs, as well as a bug bounty for universal jailbreaks.
units.paraphrase: ASL-2 requires clear in-product vulnerability reporting channels and a bug bounty for universal jailbreaks.

units.locator: App B / ASL-2 Security Standard / intro
units.excerpt: ASL-2 Security Standard: A security system that can likely thwart most opportunistic attackers.
units.paraphrase: The ASL-2 Security Standard is designed to thwart most opportunistic attackers.

units.locator: App B / ASL-2 Security Standard / item 1
units.excerpt: Supply chain: Vendor and supplier security must be regularly reviewed to ensure that they meet security standards. Software updates should be frequently managed and compliance monitoring automated where possible.
units.paraphrase: Supply chain security requires regular vendor reviews, frequent software update management, and automated compliance monitoring.

units.locator: App B / ASL-2 Security Standard / item 2
units.excerpt: Offices: Physical security should entail visitor access logs and restrictions protect on-site assets. Highly sensitive interactions should utilize advanced authentication like security keys.
units.paraphrase: Office security should include visitor logs, asset access restrictions, and advanced authentication for sensitive interactions.

units.locator: App B / ASL-2 Security Standard / item 2
units.excerpt: Network visibility should be maintained and office access controls and communications should maximize on-site protections.
units.paraphrase: Network visibility and office access controls should be maintained to maximize on-site protections.

units.locator: App B / ASL-2 Security Standard / item 3
units.excerpt: Workforce: People-critical processes must represent a key aspect of cybersecurity. Mandatory periodic infosec training educates all employees on secure practices, like proper system configurations and strong passwords, and fosters a proactive "security mindset."
units.paraphrase: Workforce security requires people-focused processes and mandatory periodic infosec training fostering a security mindset.

units.locator: App B / ASL-2 Security Standard / item 3
units.excerpt: Fundamental infrastructure and policies promoting secure-by-design and secure-by-default principles should be incorporated into the engineering process. An insider risk program should tie access to job roles. Rapid incident response protocols must be deployed.
units.paraphrase: Secure-by-design/default principles should be embedded in engineering, insider risk should be tied to job roles, and rapid incident response is required.

units.locator: App B / ASL-2 Security Standard / item 4
units.excerpt: Compartmentalization: Segmented system isolation must ensure limited blast radius. Features like zero trust architecture should require access from approved devices.
units.paraphrase: Compartmentalization requires segmented isolation limiting blast radius and zero trust architecture restricting access to approved devices.

units.locator: App B / ASL-2 Security Standard / item 4
units.excerpt: Strict protocols must be deployed to regulate weight copies on company networks and limit storage to only approved, restricted systems.
units.paraphrase: Strict protocols must govern weight copies on company networks, limiting storage to approved restricted systems.

units.locator: App B / ASL-2 Security Standard / item 5
units.excerpt: Infrastructure: Standard security infrastructure, monitoring software, access management tools, and disk encryption provide a technology baseline. Process elements like incident reporting procedures, lost/stolen device protocols and Detection and Response should support these.
units.paraphrase: Infrastructure baseline includes standard security tools, monitoring, access management and disk encryption, supported by incident and device-loss protocols.

units.locator: App B / ASL-2 Security Standard / item 5
units.excerpt: External validation like SOC 2 compliance and continuous vulnerability management must ensure adaptations match infosec developments. Programs like bug bounties and vulnerability discovery should incentivize exposing flaws.
units.paraphrase: External validation (e.g., SOC 2) and continuous vulnerability management must keep pace with infosec developments, supported by bug bounty programs.

units.locator: App B / ASL-2 Security Standard / item 6
units.excerpt: Operations: Ongoing configuration management, compliance drills, integrated security approaches and mandatory external reviews should embed security within regular operations and harden processes during organizational changes.
units.paraphrase: Operational security requires ongoing configuration management, compliance drills, and mandatory external reviews to embed security and harden processes during change.

units.excerpt: This appendix contains detailed definitions for each Capability Threshold in Section 2.
units.paraphrase: The appendix provides detailed definitions of each Capability Threshold referenced in Section 2.

units.context_stem: Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear (CBRN) weapons:
units.excerpt: CBRN-3: The ability to significantly assist individuals or groups with basic STEM backgrounds in obtaining, producing, or deploying CBRN weapons.
units.paraphrase: CBRN-3 is the capability to significantly help STEM-background actors obtain, produce, or deploy CBRN weapons.

units.excerpt: We assess this by comparing what potential attackers could achieve with full model access versus 2023-level online resources, assuming they have funding and up to one year of time to invest, but no initial specialized expertise.
units.paraphrase: Assessment compares model-assisted attacker capability against 2023-level online resources, assuming funding and up to one year, but no prior specialized expertise.

units.context_stem: Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear (CBRN) weapons:
units.excerpt: CBRN-4: The ability to substantially uplift CBRN development capabilities of moderately resourced state programs (with relevant expert teams), such as by novel weapons design, substantially accelerating existing processes, or dramatic reduction in technical barriers.
units.paraphrase: CBRN-4 is the ability to substantially advance state-level CBRN programs via novel design, acceleration, or barrier reduction.

units.excerpt: We currently define this as uplifting a team of people with skills equivalent to entry-level PhD biologists to be able to approximate the capabilities of a world-class, state-backed bioweapons team.
units.paraphrase: CBRN-4 is currently defined as uplifting entry-level PhD-equivalent biologists to approximate world-class state-backed bioweapons team capability.

units.excerpt: AI R&D-4: The ability to fully automate the work of an entry-level, remote-only Researcher at Anthropic.
units.paraphrase: AI R&D-4 is the ability to fully automate an entry-level, remote-only Anthropic researcher's work.

units.excerpt: AI R&D-5: The ability to cause dramatic acceleration in the rate of effective scaling. Specifically, this would be the case if we observed or projected an increase in the effective training compute of the world's most capable model that, over the course of a year, was equivalent to two years of the average rate of progress during the period of early 2018 to early 2024.
units.paraphrase: AI R&D-5 is the ability to dramatically accelerate scaling, defined as achieving in one year an increase equivalent to two years of the 2018-2024 average progress rate.

units.excerpt: We roughly estimate that the 2018-2024 average scaleup was around 35x per year, so this would imply an actual or projected one-year scaleup of 352 = ~1000x.
units.paraphrase: The estimated 35x/year average scaleup implies AI R&D-5 corresponds to a roughly 1000x one-year scaleup.

units.excerpt: Model Autonomy checkpoint: The ability to perform a wide range of advanced software engineering tasks autonomously that could be precursors to full autonomous replication or automated AI R&D, and that would take a domain expert human 2-8 hours to complete.
units.paraphrase: The Model Autonomy checkpoint is autonomous performance of advanced software engineering tasks taking a human expert 2-8 hours, as precursors to fuller autonomy.

units.excerpt: We primarily view this level of model autonomy as a checkpoint on the way to managing the risks of robust, fully autonomous systems with capabilities that might include (a) automating and greatly accelerating research and development in AI development (b) generating their own revenue and using it to run copies of themselves in large-scale, hard-to-shut-down operations.
units.paraphrase: This autonomy level is viewed as an intermediate checkpoint toward managing risks from fully autonomous systems capable of accelerating AI R&D or self-funding replication.

units.excerpt: We are uncertain how to choose a specific threshold, but we maintain a current list of specific CBRN capabilities of concern for which we would implement stronger mitigations.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic maintains a list of specific concerning CBRN capabilities warranting stronger mitigations, despite uncertainty on precise thresholds.

units.excerpt: We treat these lists as sensitive, but we plan to share them with organizations such as AI Safety Institutes and the Frontier Model Forum, and keep these lists updated.
units.paraphrase: These sensitive lists will be shared with bodies like AI Safety Institutes and the Frontier Model Forum and kept updated.

units.excerpt: This comparison is hard to make in practice; this note is to clarify the meaning of the conceptual threshold and the fact that this policy aims to measure risk relative to the world in 2023, so that we can understand how much risk the current generations of frontier models are creating.
units.paraphrase: This footnote clarifies that the comparison is difficult in practice, and the policy intends to measure risk relative to a 2023 baseline.

units.excerpt: The 35x/year scaleup estimate is based on assuming the rate of increase in compute being used to train frontier models from ~2018 to May 2024 is 4.2 x/year (reference), the impact of increased (LLM) algorithmic efficiency is roughly equivalent to a further 2.8 x/year (reference), and the impact of post training enhancements is a further 3 x/year (informal estimate).
units.paraphrase: The 35x/year estimate derives from combining 4.2x/year compute growth, 2.8x/year algorithmic efficiency gains, and 3x/year post-training enhancement gains.

units.excerpt: Combined, these have an effective rate of scaling of 35 x/year.
units.paraphrase: The combined effective scaling rate from all three factors is 35x per year.

units.excerpt: September 19, 2023 (RSP v1.0) RSP-2023 (aka RSP v1.0): Initial version.
units.paraphrase: The changelog records that the initial RSP version was released September 19, 2023.

units.excerpt: RSP-2024: This update introduces a more flexible and nuanced approach to assessing and managing AI risks while maintaining our commitment not to train or deploy models unless we have implemented adequate safeguards.
units.paraphrase: The 2024 update adopts a more flexible risk-management approach while retaining the commitment against training/deploying without adequate safeguards.

units.excerpt: Key improvements include new capability thresholds to indicate when we should upgrade our safeguards, refined processes for evaluating model capabilities and the adequacy of our safeguards (inspired by safety case methodologies), and new measures for internal governance and external input.
units.paraphrase: Key 2024 improvements include new capability thresholds, refined safety-case-inspired evaluation processes, and new governance and external-input measures.

units.excerpt: ASL definition changed: The term "ASL" now refers to groups of technical and operational safeguards (it previously also referred to models). We also introduced the new concepts of Capability Thresholds and Required Safeguards.
units.paraphrase: The ASL definition was changed to refer only to safeguard groups, no longer to models, alongside new Capability Thresholds and Required Safeguards concepts.

units.excerpt: This change allows for more targeted application of safeguards based on specific capabilities, rather than broad model categories.
units.paraphrase: The redefinition enables safeguards to be targeted at specific capabilities rather than broad model categories.

units.locator: Changelog / October 15, 2024 / ARA threshold now a checkpoint
units.excerpt: ARA threshold now a checkpoint: We replaced our previous autonomous replication and adaption (ARA) threshold with a "checkpoint" for autonomous AI capabilities.
units.paraphrase: The previous ARA threshold was replaced with a checkpoint concept for autonomous AI capabilities.

units.locator: Changelog / October 15, 2024 / ARA threshold now a checkpoint
units.excerpt: Rather than triggering higher safety standards automatically, reaching this checkpoint will prompt additional evaluation of the model's capabilities and accelerate our preparation of stronger safeguards.
units.paraphrase: Reaching the checkpoint prompts additional evaluation and accelerated safeguard preparation rather than automatically triggering higher standards.

units.locator: Changelog / October 15, 2024 / ARA threshold now a checkpoint
units.excerpt: We previously considered these capabilities as a trigger for increased safeguards, motivated by an attempt to establish some threshold while we developed a better sense of potential threats.
units.paraphrase: These capabilities were previously treated as a safeguard trigger as a provisional measure while understanding of threats developed.

units.locator: Changelog / October 15, 2024 / ARA threshold now a checkpoint
units.excerpt: We now believe that these capabilities - at the levels we initially considered - would not necessitate the ASL-3 standard.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic now believes these capability levels do not require the ASL-3 standard.

units.locator: Changelog / October 15, 2024 / AI R&D threshold added
units.excerpt: AI R&D threshold added: We added a new threshold for AI systems that can significantly advance AI development.
units.paraphrase: A new threshold was added for AI systems capable of significantly advancing AI development.

units.locator: Changelog / October 15, 2024 / AI R&D threshold added
units.excerpt: Such capabilities could lead to rapid, unpredictable advances in AI, potentially outpacing our ability to evaluate and address emerging risks, and may also serve as an early warning sign for the ability to automate R&D in other domains.
units.paraphrase: These capabilities risk rapid unpredictable AI advances outpacing risk evaluation, and may signal broader R&D automation potential.

units.locator: Changelog / October 15, 2024 / Testing for Capability Thresholds
units.excerpt: Testing for Capability Thresholds: Rather than using prespecified evaluations, we now require an affirmative case that models are sufficiently far from Capability Thresholds.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic now requires an affirmative case of sufficient distance from Capability Thresholds rather than relying on prespecified evaluations.

units.locator: Changelog / October 15, 2024 / Testing for Capability Thresholds
units.excerpt: Predefined tests may miss emerging risks or be overly conservative relative to the actual threshold of concern.
units.paraphrase: Predefined tests risk missing emerging risks or being overly conservative relative to actual thresholds.

units.locator: Changelog / October 15, 2024 / Testing for Capability Thresholds
units.excerpt: Our most accurate tests change frequently enough that it is more practical to use this new approach than to have our Board of Directors pre-approve evaluations.
units.paraphrase: Frequently changing best tests make the new affirmative-case approach more practical than Board pre-approval of evaluations.

units.excerpt: Adjusted evaluation cadence: We adjusted the comprehensive assessment cadence to 4x Effective Compute or six months of accumulated post-training enhancements (this was previously three months).
units.paraphrase: The assessment cadence was adjusted to 4x Effective Compute or six months of accumulated post-training enhancements, up from three months.

units.excerpt: We found that a three-month cadence forced teams to prioritize conducting frequent evaluations over more comprehensive testing and improving methodologies.
units.paraphrase: A three-month cadence had forced teams to prioritize evaluation frequency over comprehensiveness and methodology improvement.

units.locator: Changelog / October 15, 2024 / Less prescriptive evaluation methodology
units.excerpt: Less prescriptive evaluation methodology: We have replaced some specifics in our previous testing methodology (e.g., using 1% of compute for elicitation or creating a 6x buffer), with more general requirements to (a) match expected efforts of potential adversaries and (b) provide informal estimates of how further scaling and research developments will impact model capabilities and performance on the same tasks.
units.paraphrase: Specific prior methodology elements (e.g., 1% compute for elicitation, 6x buffer) were replaced with general requirements to match adversary effort and estimate future capability impacts.

units.locator: Changelog / October 15, 2024 / Less prescriptive evaluation methodology
units.excerpt: We have found that specific methodologies may become outdated when new research developments are introduced.
units.paraphrase: Specific methodologies risk becoming outdated as new research emerges.

units.locator: Changelog / October 15, 2024 / Less prescriptive evaluation methodology
units.excerpt: Although still an aspirational goal, the science of evaluations is not currently mature enough to make confident predictions about the precise buffer we should require between current models and a Capability Threshold.
units.paraphrase: Evaluation science is not yet mature enough to confidently prescribe a precise buffer between current models and a Capability Threshold, though this remains an aspiration.

units.locator: Changelog / October 15, 2024 / More outcome-focused safeguard requirements
units.excerpt: More outcome-focused safeguard requirements: We have updated our ASL-3 safeguards requirements to be less prescriptive and more outcome-focused.
units.paraphrase: ASL-3 safeguard requirements were updated to be less prescriptive and more outcome-focused.

units.locator: Changelog / October 15, 2024 / More outcome-focused safeguard requirements
units.excerpt: Rather than detailing specific operational and technical safeguards, we now specify the overall security or deployment standards and requirements for meeting them.
units.paraphrase: Instead of detailing specific safeguards, overall security/deployment standards and their requirements are now specified.

units.locator: Changelog / October 15, 2024 / More outcome-focused safeguard requirements
units.excerpt: This is to allow us to adapt our safeguards more flexibly as our understanding of risks and possible safeguards improves.
units.paraphrase: The outcome-focused approach allows more flexible safeguard adaptation as understanding improves.

units.locator: Changelog / October 15, 2024 / Clarified ASL-3 and ASL-2 security threat models
units.excerpt: Clarified ASL-3 and ASL-2 security threat models: We have clarified which actors are in and out of scope for the ASL-3 Security Standard.
units.paraphrase: The scope of actors covered by the ASL-3 Security Standard was clarified.

units.locator: Changelog / October 15, 2024 / Clarified ASL-3 and ASL-2 security threat models
units.excerpt: We also removed the commitment to protect against scaled attacks and distillation attacks from the ASL-2 Security standard.
units.paraphrase: The commitment to protect against scaled and distillation attacks was removed from the ASL-2 Security Standard.

units.locator: Changelog / October 15, 2024 / Clarified ASL-3 and ASL-2 security threat models
units.excerpt: While distillation remains a concern for more capable models, models stored under ASL-2 safeguards have not yet reached potentially harmful Capability Thresholds.
units.paraphrase: Distillation remains a concern for more capable models, but ASL-2 models have not reached potentially harmful Capability Thresholds.

units.locator: Changelog / October 15, 2024 / Clarified requirements for deployments with trusted users
units.excerpt: Clarified requirements for deployments with trusted users: We have updated the ASL-3 Deployment Standard to allow for different levels of safeguards based on deployment context.
units.paraphrase: The ASL-3 Deployment Standard was updated to allow safeguard levels to vary by deployment context.

units.locator: Changelog / October 15, 2024 / Clarified requirements for deployments with trusted users
units.excerpt: For any general access systems, we still require passing intensive red-teaming. For internal use, safety testing and deployments to sufficiently trusted users, we will instead require a combination of access controls and monitoring.
units.paraphrase: General access systems still require intensive red-teaming, while internal use and trusted-user deployments instead require access controls and monitoring.

units.locator: Changelog / October 15, 2024 / New Capability and Safeguards Reports
units.excerpt: New Capability and Safeguards Reports: We have introduced Capability Reports and Safeguard Reports.
units.paraphrase: Capability Reports and Safeguard Reports were newly introduced.

units.locator: Changelog / October 15, 2024 / New Capability and Safeguards Reports
units.excerpt: We expect that aggregating all the available evidence about model capabilities will provide decision makers with a more complete picture of the overall level of risk and improve our ability to solicit feedback on our work.
units.paraphrase: Aggregating capability evidence is expected to give decision-makers a fuller risk picture and improve feedback-seeking.

units.locator: Changelog / October 15, 2024 / Internal and external accountability
units.excerpt: Internal and external accountability: We have made a number of changes to our previous "procedural commitments." These include expanding the duties of the Responsible Scaling Officer; adding internal critique and external expert input on capability and safeguard assessments; new procedures related to internal governance;
units.paraphrase: Procedural commitments were changed to expand RSO duties, add internal/external review input, and introduce new internal governance procedures.

units.locator: Changelog / October 15, 2024 / Internal and external accountability
units.excerpt: and maintaining a public page for overviews of past Capability and Safeguard Reports, RSP-related updates, and future plans.
units.paraphrase: A public page will also be maintained summarizing past reports, RSP updates, and future plans.

units.excerpt: RSP-2025: This update clarifies which Capability Thresholds would require enhanced safeguards beyond our current ASL-3 standards.
units.paraphrase: The 2025 update clarifies which Capability Thresholds require safeguards beyond the current ASL-3 standard.

units.excerpt: New Capability Thresholds: We have added a new capability threshold related to CBRN development, which defines capabilities that could substantially uplift the development capabilities of moderately resourced state programs.
units.paraphrase: A new CBRN-related capability threshold was added defining substantial uplift to moderately resourced state programs.

units.excerpt: We have also disaggregated our existing AI R&D capability thresholds, separating them into two distinct levels (the ability to fully automate entry-level AI research work, and the ability to cause dramatic acceleration in the rate of effective scaling) and provided additional detail on the corresponding Required Safeguards.
units.paraphrase: Existing AI R&D thresholds were split into two levels—full automation of entry-level research and dramatic scaling acceleration—with added detail on Required Safeguards.

units.excerpt: Iterative Commitment: We have adopted a general commitment to reevaluate our Capability Thresholds whenever we upgrade to a new set of Required Safeguards.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic commits to reevaluating Capability Thresholds each time Required Safeguards are upgraded.

units.excerpt: We have decided not to maintain a commitment to define ASL-N+1 evaluations by the time we develop ASL-N models; such an approach would add unnecessary complexity because Capability Thresholds do not naturally come grouped in discrete levels.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic dropped the commitment to pre-define next-level evaluations by the time current-level models are developed, since thresholds do not group into discrete levels naturally.

units.excerpt: We believe it is more practical and sensible instead to commit to reconsidering the whole list of Capability Thresholds whenever we upgrade our safeguards.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic prefers reconsidering the entire list of Capability Thresholds whenever safeguards are upgraded, as more practical.

excerpt: In September 2023, we released our Responsible Scaling Policy (RSP), a public commitment not to train or deploy models capable of causing catastrophic harm unless we have implemented safety and security measures that will keep risks below acceptable levels.
paraphrase: Anthropic states that in September 2023 it released the RSP, a public commitment to avoid training or deploying catastrophically harmful models absent adequate safety and security measures.

excerpt: We are now updating our RSP to account for the lessons we've learned over the last year.
paraphrase: Anthropic notes it is updating the RSP based on lessons learned over the past year.

excerpt: This updated policy reflects our view that risk governance in this rapidly evolving domain should be proportional, iterative, and exportable.
paraphrase: Anthropic frames its updated risk governance approach as proportional, iterative, and exportable.

excerpt: Background. AI Safety Level Standards (ASL Standards) are a set of technical and operational measures for safely training and deploying frontier AI models.
paraphrase: ASL Standards are defined as technical and operational measures for safe training and deployment of frontier AI models.

excerpt: These currently fall into two categories: Deployment Standards and Security Standards.
paraphrase: ASL Standards are divided into Deployment Standards and Security Standards.

excerpt: As model capabilities increase, so will the need for stronger safeguards, which are captured in successively higher ASL Standards.
paraphrase: Stronger safeguards, reflected in higher ASL Standards, will be needed as model capabilities increase.

excerpt: At present, all of our models must meet the ASL-2 Deployment and Security Standards.
paraphrase: All current models are required to meet the ASL-2 Deployment and Security Standards.

excerpt: To determine when a model has become sufficiently advanced such that its deployment and security measures should be strengthened, we use the concepts of Capability Thresholds and Required Safeguards.
paraphrase: Capability Thresholds and Required Safeguards are the concepts used to decide when to strengthen deployment and security measures.

excerpt: A Capability Threshold tells us when we need to upgrade our protections, and the corresponding Required Safeguards tell us what standard should apply.
paraphrase: A Capability Threshold indicates timing for upgrading protections, while Required Safeguards indicate which standard applies.

excerpt: Capability Thresholds and Required Safeguards. The Required Safeguards for each Capability Threshold are intended to mitigate risk to acceptable levels.
paraphrase: Required Safeguards for each Capability Threshold aim to mitigate risk to acceptable levels.

excerpt: This update to our RSP provides specifications for Capabilities Thresholds related to Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear (CBRN) weapons and Autonomous AI Research and Development (AI R&D) and identifies the corresponding Required Safeguards.
paraphrase: The updated RSP specifies Capability Thresholds for CBRN weapons and Autonomous AI R&D, along with their corresponding Required Safeguards.

excerpt: Capability assessment. We will routinely test models to determine whether their capabilities fall sufficiently far below the Capability Thresholds such that the ASL-2 Standard remains appropriate.
paraphrase: Anthropic commits to routinely testing models to check whether ASL-2 remains sufficient.

excerpt: We will first conduct preliminary assessments to determine whether a more comprehensive evaluation is needed.
paraphrase: Preliminary assessments will be conducted first to determine the need for comprehensive evaluation.

excerpt: For models requiring comprehensive testing, we will assess whether the model is unlikely to reach any relevant Capability Thresholds absent surprising advances in widely accessible post-training enhancements.
paraphrase: For models needing comprehensive testing, Anthropic will assess whether the model is unlikely to reach relevant Capability Thresholds barring unexpected advances in accessible post-training techniques.

excerpt: If, after the comprehensive testing, we determine that the model is sufficiently below the relevant Capability Thresholds, then we will continue to apply the ASL-2 Standard.
paraphrase: If comprehensive testing shows the model is sufficiently below the thresholds, ASL-2 continues to apply.

excerpt: If, however, we are unable to make the required showing, we will act as though the model has surpassed the Capability Threshold.
paraphrase: If the required showing cannot be made, Anthropic will treat the model as having surpassed the Capability Threshold.

excerpt: This means that we will both upgrade to the ASL-3 Required Safeguards and conduct a follow-up capability assessment to confirm that the ASL-4 Standard is not necessary.
paraphrase: Treating the model as having surpassed the threshold triggers both an upgrade to ASL-3 Required Safeguards and a follow-up assessment to rule out the need for ASL-4.

excerpt: Safeguards assessment. To determine whether the measures we have adopted satisfy the ASL-3 Required Safeguards, we will conduct a safeguards assessment.
paraphrase: Anthropic will conduct a safeguards assessment to check whether adopted measures satisfy ASL-3 Required Safeguards.

excerpt: For the ASL-3 Deployment Standard, we will evaluate whether it is robust to persistent attempts to misuse the capability in question.
paraphrase: The ASL-3 Deployment Standard evaluation checks robustness against persistent misuse attempts.

excerpt: For the ASL-3 Security Standard, we will evaluate whether it is highly protected against non-state attackers attempting to steal model weights.
paraphrase: The ASL-3 Security Standard evaluation checks protection against non-state actors attempting weight theft.

excerpt: If we determine that we have met the ASL-3 Required Safeguards, then we will proceed to deployment, provided we have also conducted a follow-up capability assessment.
paraphrase: Deployment proceeds once ASL-3 Required Safeguards are met and a follow-up capability assessment has been conducted.

excerpt: Follow-up capability assessment. In parallel with upgrading a model to the ASL-3 Required Safeguards, we will conduct a follow-up capability assessment to confirm that further safeguards are not necessary.
paraphrase: While upgrading to ASL-3 Required Safeguards, a follow-up capability assessment will confirm whether further safeguards are needed.

excerpt: Deployment and scaling outcomes. We may deploy or store a model if either of the following criteria are met: (1) the model's capabilities are sufficiently far away from the existing Capability Thresholds, making the current ASL-2 Standard appropriate;
paraphrase: A model may be deployed or stored if its capabilities are sufficiently far from existing Capability Thresholds, keeping ASL-2 appropriate.

context_stem: We may deploy or store a model if either of the following criteria are met
excerpt: or (2) the model's capabilities have surpassed the existing Capabilities Threshold, but we have implemented the ASL-3 Required Safeguards and conducted the follow-up capability assessment.
paraphrase: Alternatively, a model may be deployed or stored if it has surpassed the Capability Threshold but ASL-3 Required Safeguards and a follow-up assessment are in place.

excerpt: In any scenario where we determine that a model requires ASL-3 Required Safeguards but we are unable to implement them immediately, we will act promptly to reduce interim risk to acceptable levels until the ASL-3 Required Safeguards are in place.
paraphrase: If ASL-3 Required Safeguards cannot be implemented immediately, Anthropic commits to promptly reducing interim risk until they are in place.

excerpt: Governance and transparency. To facilitate the effective implementation of this policy across the company, we commit to several internal governance measures, including maintaining the position of Responsible Scaling Officer, establishing a process through which Anthropic staff may anonymously notify the Responsible Scaling Officer of any potential instances of noncompliance, and developing internal safety procedures for incident scenarios.
paraphrase: Anthropic commits to internal governance measures including a Responsible Scaling Officer role, an anonymous noncompliance reporting channel, and internal incident procedures.

excerpt: To advance the public dialogue on the regulation of frontier AI model risks and to enable examination of our actions, we will also publicly release key materials related to the evaluation and deployment of our models with sensitive information removed and solicit input from external experts in relevant domains.
paraphrase: Anthropic commits to publicly releasing evaluation and deployment materials, redacted of sensitive information, and to seeking external expert input.

excerpt: As frontier AI models advance, we believe they will bring about transformative benefits for our society and economy.
paraphrase: Anthropic states its belief that advancing frontier AI models will bring transformative societal and economic benefits.

excerpt: AI could accelerate scientific discoveries, revolutionize healthcare, enhance our education system, and create entirely new domains for human creativity and innovation.
paraphrase: AI is described as potentially accelerating science, healthcare, education, and creativity.

excerpt: Frontier AI models also, however, present new challenges and risks that warrant careful study and effective safeguards.
paraphrase: Frontier AI models also pose new risks requiring careful study and effective safeguards.

excerpt: In September 2023, we released our Responsible Scaling Policy (RSP), a first-of-its-kind public commitment not to train or deploy models capable of causing catastrophic harm unless we have implemented safety and security measures that will keep risks below acceptable levels.
paraphrase: Anthropic reiterates the original 2023 RSP commitment against training or deploying catastrophically dangerous models without adequate safety and security measures.

excerpt: Our RSP serves several purposes: it is an internal operating procedure for investigating and mitigating these risks and helps inform the public of our plans and commitments.
paraphrase: The RSP serves as both an internal operating procedure and a public communication of Anthropic's plans and commitments.

excerpt: We also hope it will serve as a prototype for other companies looking to adopt similar frameworks and, potentially, inform regulators about possible best practices.
paraphrase: Anthropic hopes the RSP can serve as a model for other companies and inform regulatory best practices.

excerpt: We are now updating our RSP to account for the lessons we've learned over the last year.
paraphrase: Anthropic reiterates that the RSP is being updated based on lessons learned.

excerpt: This policy reflects our view that risk governance in this rapidly evolving domain should be proportional, iterative, and exportable.
paraphrase: The policy reflects the view that risk governance should be proportional, iterative, and exportable.

excerpt: First, our approach to risk should be proportional. Central to our policy is the concept of AI Safety Level Standards: technical and operational standards for safely training and deploying frontier models that correspond with a particular level of risk.
paraphrase: The proportionality principle centers on AI Safety Level Standards that scale with the level of risk posed by a model.

excerpt: By implementing safeguards that are proportional to the nature and extent of an AI model's risks, we can balance innovation with safety, maintaining rigorous protections without unnecessarily hindering progress.
paraphrase: Proportional safeguards are intended to balance safety and innovation without unnecessary hindrance.

excerpt: This approach also enables us to allocate resources efficiently, focusing our most stringent safeguards on the models that pose the greater risk, while affording more flexibility for lower-risk systems.
paraphrase: The proportional approach lets Anthropic focus stringent safeguards on higher-risk models and allow flexibility for lower-risk systems.

excerpt: Second, our approach to risk should be iterative. Since the frontier of AI is rapidly evolving, we cannot anticipate what safety and security measures will be appropriate for models far beyond the current frontier.
paraphrase: The iterative principle acknowledges that future safety measures cannot be fully anticipated given rapid AI progress.

excerpt: We will thus regularly measure the capability of our models and adjust our safeguards accordingly.
paraphrase: Anthropic will regularly measure model capability and adjust safeguards accordingly.

excerpt: Further, we will continue to research potential risks and next-generation mitigation techniques.
paraphrase: Anthropic will continue researching potential risks and future mitigation techniques.

excerpt: And, at the highest level of generality, we will look for opportunities to improve and strengthen our overarching risk management framework.
paraphrase: Anthropic will seek opportunities to strengthen its overall risk management framework.

excerpt: Third, our approach to risk should be exportable. To demonstrate that it is possible to balance innovation with safety, we must put forward our proof of concept: a pragmatic, flexible, and scalable approach to risk governance.
paraphrase: The exportability principle involves presenting a pragmatic, scalable risk governance model as proof that innovation and safety can coexist.

excerpt: By sharing our approach externally, we aim to set a new industry standard that encourages widespread adoption of similar frameworks.
paraphrase: Sharing the approach externally aims to set an industry standard encouraging wider adoption.

excerpt: In the long term, we hope that our policy may offer relevant insights for regulation.
paraphrase: Anthropic hopes the policy could inform future regulation over the long term.

excerpt: In the meantime, we will continue to share our findings with policymakers.
paraphrase: Anthropic will continue sharing findings with policymakers in the interim.

excerpt: Although this policy focuses on catastrophic risks, they are not the only risks that we consider important.
paraphrase: Anthropic notes that catastrophic risks are the focus of this policy but not the only risks it considers important.

excerpt: Our Usage Policy sets forth our standards for the use of our products, including prohibitions on using our models to spread misinformation, incite violence or hateful behavior, or engage in fraudulent or abusive practices, and we continually refine our technical measures for enforcing our trust and safety standards at scale.
paraphrase: The separate Usage Policy prohibits misuse such as misinformation, incitement, and fraud, and Anthropic continually refines enforcement measures.

excerpt: Further, we conduct research to understand the broader societal impacts of our models.
paraphrase: Anthropic conducts research into broader societal impacts of its models.

excerpt: Our Responsible Scaling Policy complements our work in these areas, contributing to our understanding of current and potential risks.
paraphrase: The RSP is described as complementary to other risk-related work at Anthropic.

excerpt: At Anthropic, we are committed to developing AI responsibly and transparently.
paraphrase: Anthropic states its commitment to responsible and transparent AI development.

excerpt: Since our founding, we have recognized the importance of proactively addressing potential risks as we push the boundaries of AI capability and of clearly communicating about the nature and extent of those risks.
paraphrase: Anthropic states it has long recognized the importance of proactive risk management and clear communication about risk.

excerpt: We look forward to continuing to refine our approach to risk governance and to collaborating with stakeholders across the AI ecosystem.
paraphrase: Anthropic expresses intent to keep refining its risk governance and to collaborate with ecosystem stakeholders.

excerpt: This policy is designed in the spirit of the Responsible Scaling Policy (RSP) framework introduced by the non-profit AI safety organization METR, as well as emerging government policy proposals in the UK, EU, and US.
paraphrase: The policy is framed as inspired by METR's RSP framework and emerging UK, EU, and US government policy proposals.

excerpt: This policy also helps satisfy our Voluntary White House Commitments (2023) and Frontier AI Safety Commitments (2024).
paraphrase: The policy is also said to help satisfy the 2023 Voluntary White House Commitments and 2024 Frontier AI Safety Commitments.

excerpt: We extend our sincere gratitude to the many external groups that provided invaluable guidance on the development and refinement of our Responsible Scaling Policy.
paraphrase: Anthropic thanks external groups for input on developing the RSP.

excerpt: We actively welcome feedback on our policy and suggestions for improvement from other entities engaged in frontier AI risk evaluations or safety and security standards.
paraphrase: Anthropic invites feedback from other organizations working on frontier AI risk and safety standards.

excerpt: To submit your feedback or suggestions, please contact us at rsp@anthropic.com.
paraphrase: Feedback and suggestions can be submitted to a provided contact email.

excerpt: AI Safety Level Standards (ASL Standards) are core to our risk mitigation strategy. An ASL Standard is a set of technical and operational measures for safely training and deploying frontier AI models.
paraphrase: ASL Standards are core to Anthropic's risk mitigation and are defined as technical and operational measures for safe training and deployment.

excerpt: As model capabilities increase, so will the need for stronger safeguards, which are captured in successively higher ASL Standards.
paraphrase: Higher capabilities require stronger safeguards, reflected in successively higher ASL Standards.

excerpt: Definitions of ASL Standards and other key terms are available in Appendix A.
paraphrase: Appendix A contains definitions of ASL Standards and other key terms.

excerpt: The types of measures that compose an ASL Standard currently fall into two categories–Deployment Standards and Security Standards–which map onto the types of risks that frontier AI models may pose.
paraphrase: ASL Standards consist of Deployment Standards and Security Standards, each mapping onto different risk types.

excerpt: Deployment Standards: Deployment Standards are technical, operational, and policy measures to ensure the safe usage of AI models by external users (i.e., our users and customers) as well as internal users (i.e., our employees).
paraphrase: Deployment Standards are defined as measures ensuring safe use of AI models by both external and internal users.

excerpt: Deployment Standards aim to strike a balance between enabling beneficial use of AI technologies and mitigating the risks of potentially catastrophic cases of misuse.
paraphrase: Deployment Standards seek to balance beneficial use against catastrophic misuse risk.

excerpt: Security Standards: Security Standards are technical, operational, and policy measures to protect AI models–particularly their weights and associated systems–from unauthorized access, theft, or compromise by malicious actors.
paraphrase: Security Standards are defined as measures protecting AI models, especially weights, from unauthorized access or theft.

excerpt: Security Standards are intended to maintain the integrity and controlled use of AI models throughout their lifecycle, from development to deployment.
paraphrase: Security Standards aim to preserve model integrity and controlled use across the model lifecycle.

excerpt: We expect to continue refining our framework in response to future risks (for example, the risk that an AI system attempts to subvert the goals of its operators).
paraphrase: Anthropic expects to keep refining its framework to address future risks such as an AI subverting operator goals.

excerpt: At present, all of our models must meet the ASL-2 Deployment and Security Standards. The ASL-2 Security and Deployment Standards provide a baseline level of safe deployment and model security for AI models.
paraphrase: All current models must meet ASL-2 standards, which provide baseline safety and security.

excerpt: These standards, which are summarized below, are available in full in Appendix B.
paraphrase: The full ASL-2 standards are located in Appendix B, with a summary given here.

excerpt: The ASL-2 Deployment Standard reduces the prevalence of misuse, and includes the publication of model cards and enforcement of Usage Policy; harmlessness training such as Constitutional AI and automated detection mechanisms; and establishing vulnerability reporting channels as well as a bug bounty for universal jailbreaks.
paraphrase: ASL-2 Deployment Standard includes model card publication, Usage Policy enforcement, harmlessness training, detection mechanisms, vulnerability reporting, and a jailbreak bug bounty.

excerpt: The ASL-2 Security Standard requires a security system that can likely thwart most opportunistic attackers and includes vendor and supplier security reviews, physical security measures, and the use of secure-by-design principles.
paraphrase: ASL-2 Security Standard requires defenses against most opportunistic attackers, plus vendor reviews, physical security, and secure-by-design practices.

excerpt: Although the ASL-2 Standard is appropriate for all of our current models, that may not hold true in the future as our models become more capable.
paraphrase: ASL-2 is currently sufficient but may not remain so as models grow more capable.

excerpt: To determine when a model has become sufficiently advanced such that its deployment and security measures should be strengthened, we use the concepts of Capability Thresholds and Required Safeguards.
paraphrase: Capability Thresholds and Required Safeguards determine when safeguards should be strengthened.

excerpt: A Capability Threshold tells us when we need to upgrade our protections, and the corresponding Required Safeguards tell us what standard should apply.
paraphrase: A Capability Threshold signals timing for upgrading protections; Required Safeguards specify which standard applies.

excerpt: A Capability Threshold is a prespecified level of AI capability that, if reached, signals (1) a meaningful increase in the level of risk if the model remains under the existing set of safeguards and (2) a corresponding need to upgrade the safeguards to a higher ASL Standard.
paraphrase: A Capability Threshold is defined as a preset capability level signaling both increased risk and a need for higher safeguards.

excerpt: In other words, a Capability Threshold serves as a trigger for shifting from an ASL-N Standard to an ASL-N+1 Standard (or, in some cases, moving straight to ASL N+2 or higher).
paraphrase: A Capability Threshold triggers a shift from one ASL Standard to the next, or occasionally a jump of more than one level.

excerpt: Depending on the Capability Threshold, it may not be necessary to upgrade both the Deployment and Security Standards; each Capability Threshold corresponds to specific Required Safeguards that identify which of the ASL Standards must be met.
paraphrase: Not every Capability Threshold requires upgrading both standards; each threshold maps to specific Required Safeguards identifying which standards apply.

excerpt: Below, we specify the Capability Thresholds and their corresponding Required Safeguards. The Required Safeguards for each Capability Threshold are intended to mitigate risk from a model with such capabilities to acceptable levels.
paraphrase: This section specifies Capability Thresholds and Required Safeguards intended to mitigate risk to acceptable levels.

excerpt: In developing these standards, we have weighed the risks and benefits of frontier model development.
paraphrase: Anthropic states it weighed risks and benefits of frontier model development in creating these standards.

excerpt: We believe these safeguards are achievable with sufficient investment and advance planning into research and development and would advocate for the industry as a whole to adopt them.
paraphrase: Anthropic believes the safeguards are achievable with investment and planning, and advocates industry-wide adoption.

excerpt: We will conduct assessments to inform when to implement the Required Safeguards (see Section 4).
paraphrase: Assessments will determine the timing for implementing Required Safeguards.

excerpt: The Capability Thresholds summarized below are available in full in Appendix C.
paraphrase: Full Capability Thresholds are located in Appendix C, summarized in the following table.
